title: 📚 Era 3 Works: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era
subtitle: Verify publication dates, summaries, characters, storylines & exam traps for 115 works

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Bowge of Court

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 1499 (Sort Year: 1499)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Skelton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream satire in which Drede meets flattery and deceit aboard a court ship.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Poetry Foundation dates The Bouge of Court about 1499. Wynkyn de Worde printed it around 1499, while Skelton was alive. Bouge means court rations, the food and drink allowed at court. The same poem is also stored as john-skelton-bowge-of-court.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Drede (The fearful dreamer who wants favor and meets the court vices); Favell (Flattery, the first vice to welcome Drede); Deceit (One of the seven shipboard vices who turns on the dreamer); Disdain (A scornful court vice aboard the ship)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In autumn, when the sun is in Virgo, the poet falls asleep.
He dreams he is Drede, a nervous man seeking favor at court.
He boards the ship Bowge of Court, a ship of court rations and reward.
Seven vices, including flattery and deceit, befriend him and then betray him.
He is about to leap overboard when he wakes and writes the warning.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Colloquies

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1518 (Sort Year: 1518)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Desiderius Erasmus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short Latin talks that teach spoken Latin and later mock superstition and social folly.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A first edition appeared in 1518. The first edition Erasmus fully stood behind came in 1519. He enlarged the book for many years. This is a different work from Praise of Folly.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Antony (A speaker in The Shipwreck who listens in fear); Adolphus (A speaker in The Shipwreck who tells the story of the storm)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Erasmus wrote model talks so students could speak easy Latin.
A first printed book of these talks appeared in 1518.
An edition he approved followed in 1519.
He added many new talks in later years, up to the 1530s.
Talks such as The Shipwreck laugh at panic, superstition, and empty vows.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: English New Testament

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1526 (Sort Year: 1526)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Tyndale

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first complete printed New Testament in English, made from the Greek.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period start, not the book. The full Worms edition is 1526. An unfinished Cologne printing is 1525. A thorough revision was printed at Antwerp in 1534. The edition trap in the database is right.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tyndale began the work in 1523 because English readers could not have a printed Bible.
Bishop Cuthbert Tunstall would not support him, so he left for Germany in 1524.
Printing at Cologne in 1525 was stopped, and he fled to Worms.
Peter Schoeffer printed the first full edition at Worms in 1526.
Copies were smuggled into England and burned.
Tyndale revised the book in 1534.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pentateuch translation

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1530 (Sort Year: 1530)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Tyndale

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Tyndale's English Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, printed in 1530.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not the publication year. Britannica, Hertford College, and Wikipedia agree on 1530. Britannica says Marburg, which is the false imprint. Wikipedia places the press at Antwerp.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After the New Testament, Tyndale learned Hebrew and turned to the Old Testament.
In 1530 he printed the five books of Moses, each with its own title page.
The title page names Hans Lufft at Marburg, but that imprint is false.
The books were printed at Antwerp by Merten de Keyser.
These five books later fed Coverdale's Bible and the King James Bible.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Praise of Folly

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1511 (Sort Year: 1511)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Desiderius Erasmus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The goddess Folly gives a mocking speech in praise of herself and of human foolishness.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Erasmus wrote it in 1509. Gilles de Gourmont first printed it in 1511. He revised it in later editions up to 1532. The first English translation appeared in 1549. The Latin title is Moriae Encomium, also called Stultitiae Laus.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Folly (The goddess speaker, called Stultitia in Latin, who praises foolishness)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Folly steps up and says she will praise herself.
Erasmus wrote the speech in 1509, in Latin, with Thomas More in mind.
The title Moriae Encomium also plays on the name More.
Folly claims that pleasure, love, and even happy ignorance need her.
She then mocks scholars, monks, and rulers who think themselves wise.
The first printing was in Paris in 1511. An English print followed in 1549.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sonnets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1557 (Sort Year: 1557)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Love poems and moral poems, many in the English sonnet, printed after his death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Most of these poems were first printed in Tottel's Miscellany (Songes and Sonettes) in 1557, after Surrey died in 1547. The posthumous tag fits that collection. One elegy on Wyatt appeared in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The lover (The poet who praises, misses, or mourns his beloved); Thomas Wyatt (The older poet whom Surrey praises in an elegy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Surrey read Petrarch and turned Italian sonnets into smoother English.
He used three groups of four lines, then a rhyming pair.
The poems speak of love, friendship, youth, and a quiet life.
An elegy (a funeral poem) on Wyatt was printed while Surrey lived.
Richard Tottel printed forty of Surrey's poems in 1557.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sonnets after Petrarch

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1557 (Sort Year: 1557)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Wyatt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English sonnets that rewrite Petrarch's Italian love poems in Wyatt's own harsh court voice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: These sonnets were written in his lifetime and copied by hand. The first major printed book that names him is Tottel's Miscellany in 1557, fifteen years after his death. Some poems may have appeared without his name in The Court of Venus.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Lover (The speaking voice, a man caught between desire, fear, and court service)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Wyatt read love sonnets by the Italian poet Petrarch.
He kept the 14 line shape, but he often closed with a rhyming pair.
The speaker is a lover who cannot rest, like a ship in a storm.
The poems were copied by hand at court during his life.
Readers met a large group of them in Tottel's Miscellany in 1557.

items.title: "The Arte of English Poesie" (1589) — George Puttenham

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Arte of English Poesie

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1589 (Sort Year: 1589)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Puttenham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An Elizabethan handbook that defines the poet and explains English verse, measure, and figures of speech.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Richard Field printed it in London. The title page gives no author. George Puttenham is the usual name. Richard Puttenham and John, Lord Lumley, have also been suggested.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Critic (The unnamed speaking voice of the 1589 book, usually identified as George Puttenham)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The first book asks what a poet is and defends poetry.
Puttenham says a poet is a maker, not a mere translator.
The second book explains proportion, which means measure, stanza shape, and pattern.
The third book lists ornaments, which means figures of speech, and ends on decorum.
The book speaks to courtiers and often addresses Queen Elizabeth.

items.title: "The Book Named the Governor" (1531) — Thomas Elyot

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Book Named the Governor

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1531 (Sort Year: 1531)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Elyot

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A plan for educating gentlemen who will hold power in the state.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Thomas Berthelet printed the book in 1531. It was dedicated to Henry VIII. Further editions followed, including prints in 1534 and 1536.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Thomas Elyot (The author, writing to the king about education); The governor (The gentleman prepared for public office); Titus and Gisippus (Two friends in a story Elyot retells)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Elyot dedicates the book to King Henry VIII.
He says a public weal (a state) needs rulers trained in virtue.
He sets studies in Latin, Greek, history, and moral philosophy.
He also wants music, drawing, riding, wrestling, and dancing.
He retells old stories, including the friendship of Titus and Gisippus.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Scholemaster

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1570 (Sort Year: 1570)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Roger Ascham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose book on gentle teaching of Latin for boys in gentlemen's houses.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Ascham began the book in 1563. It was printed in 1570, after his death in 1568. His widow, Margaret Ascham, published it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Roger Ascham (The writer, who sets out the right way to teach); Richard Sackville (The courtier who asked Ascham to write the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1563 at Windsor, Sir Richard Sackville asked Ascham how a boy should be taught.
Sackville said a cruel master had made him hate learning.
Ascham praises kindness, praise, and a love of study.
He teaches Latin by double translation of a model such as Cicero (a Roman prose writer).
He warns that Italy can tempt young Englishmen into bad habits.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Utopia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1516 (Sort Year: 1516)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas More

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Latin story of an imagined island that mocks the greed of Europe.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Latin book was printed at Leuven in 1516. Ralph Robinson's English version came in 1551, after More's death. A revised Latin text appeared in 1518.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Raphael Hythloday (The traveller who describes the island. Latin texts call him Hythlodaeus.); Thomas More (The narrator who listens and then doubts the plan.); Peter Giles (The Antwerp friend who introduces Raphael to More.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It opens with historical event, a delegation to Bruges in 1515 in which Thomas More has taken part.
Frist book describes the oppressive injustices of England.
Second book contrasts England with Utopia described by the protagonist Raphael Hythlodaeus whom More claims to have met at Antwerp.
In Utopia there is a complete freedom of individual in social and religious spheres.
In the islands of Utopia elected representatives were called Syphograntus and Traniborus, above whom is the Prince.
No privacy or private ownership, goods are stored in warehouses, there are no lock and doors. Houses are rotated between citizens every ten years.
The favorite time pass of Utopia were music, conversations, and public lectures.
More meets the traveller Raphael Hythloday in Antwerp.
Raphael attacks war, the hanging of thieves, and enclosure (closing shared fields for sheep).
He says this greed drives poor people off the land.
Book 2 describes Utopia, an island whose name means nowhere.
The people there share goods and work only a short day.
More then doubts that such a plan can guide real kings.

items.title: "blank-verse translation of Virgil" (1557) — Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: blank-verse translation of Virgil

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1557 (Sort Year: 1557)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Surrey's English blank verse version of Virgil, the first blank verse in English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: They are one project. Tottel printed Certain Bokes of Virgiles Aenaeis in 1557. That book holds Books II and IV. Book IV had also been printed alone by John Day in 1554.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aeneas (The Trojan hero who tells Queen Dido about the fall of Troy); Dido (The queen of Carthage who loves Aeneas and is then left behind)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Virgil's Aeneid is a Latin epic (a long heroic poem) about Prince Aeneas.
Surrey turned parts of it into English lines that do not rhyme.
Each line has ten syllables, in five pairs of light and heavy stress.
He learned the idea of unrhymed verse from Italian practice.
The books were printed after his death, so he never saw them in print.

items.title: "translation of Books II and IV of the Aeneid" (1557) — Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: translation of Books II and IV of the Aeneid

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1557 (Sort Year: 1557)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Surrey's English blank verse version of two books of Virgil's Aeneid.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The posthumous tag and the translation tag are right. John Day printed Book IV in 1554 as The Fourth Boke of Virgill. Richard Tottel printed Books II and IV together in 1557 as Certain Bokes of Virgiles Aenaeis. Book II is known from that 1557 book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aeneas (The Trojan prince who survives Troy and leaves Dido); Dido (The queen whose love and death fill Book IV)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Book II tells how the Greeks took Troy with a wooden horse.
Aeneas escapes with his father and his son.
Book IV tells how Queen Dido loves Aeneas at Carthage.
Aeneas leaves her to seek Italy, and Dido kills herself.
Book IV was printed alone in 1554, and both books were printed together in 1557.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: “They Flee from Me”

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1557 (Sort Year: 1557)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Wyatt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lover remembers women who once sought him and now leave him for new faces.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That warning is right. The poem circulated in manuscript before his death in 1542. It was printed in Tottel's Miscellany in 1557. Tottel also smoothed some of Wyatt's lines.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A lover looking back on affection that has turned cold); The Woman (A remembered lover who once kissed him and now is strange and wild)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker says the women who once came to him now flee.
He remembers one woman who caught him and kissed him.
He asks if this new, cold manner is fair.
The poem uses a gentle, bitter tone, not a loud complaint.
It was copied by hand in his life and later printed in Tottel's Miscellany.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: “Whoso List to Hunt”

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1557 (Sort Year: 1557)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Wyatt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The speaker is tired of hunting a deer that already belongs to a powerful man.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: No exact writing day is known. Scholars place it in the late 1520s or early 1530s. It was printed in Tottel's Miscellany in 1557, after Wyatt died in 1542.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A tired hunter who gives up the chase); The Hind (The deer, a figure of a woman claimed by a greater power)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker tells others they may hunt a certain hind (a female deer) if they wish.
He has wasted his time in that chase and is now behind.
The deer wears a collar set with diamonds.
The collar says no one may touch her, because she is Caesar's.
The poem is Wyatt's English version of a Petrarch sonnet about a white deer.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Toxophilus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1545 (Sort Year: 1545)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Roger Ascham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dialogue in praise of archery, and a model of plain English prose.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That tag belongs to The Scholemaster of 1570. This was the first English book on archery.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Toxophilus (The lover of the bow, who defends archery); Philologus (The lover of learning, who doubts that shooting is useful)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title means lover of the bow.
Toxophilus loves shooting, and Philologus loves books.
Philologus thinks archery wastes a scholar's time.
Toxophilus defends the long bow as healthy, useful, and fit for a gentleman.
Ascham also shows that serious matter can be written in English.
He gave the book to Henry VIII and received a yearly pension.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: David and Bethsabe

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1599 (Sort Year: 1599)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Peele

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Bible play on King David, Bethsabe, and the revolt and death of Absalom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Adam Islip printed the play in 1599, after Peele died. It was entered for printing in 1594. The year of writing is not certain.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David (The king who takes Bethsabe and later mourns Absalom); Bethsabe (The woman David sees bathing, also called Bathsheba); Uriah (Bethsabe's husband, sent to die in battle); Nathan (The prophet who rebukes David's sin); Absalom (David's son, who rebels and is killed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King David sees Bethsabe bathing and takes her as his lover.
He sends her husband Uriah into battle so that Uriah will die.
The prophet Nathan rebukes David, and the couple's child dies.
David's son Absalom rebels against him and is killed.
David grieves for Absalom, and the play follows this Bible story closely.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Doctor Faustus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1604 (A text), 1616 (B text) (Sort Year: 1604)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christopher Marlowe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A scholar sells his soul to the devil for twenty four years of magic and power.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play is posthumous in print. The first surviving book is the 1604 A text. The longer B text is 1616. Performances are recorded from 1594.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Doctor Faustus (A proud scholar who bargains with the devil); Mephistophilis (The devil who serves Faustus and warns him about hell); Lucifer (The prince of devils, who claims Faustus at the end); Helen of Troy (A spirit in Helen's shape, whom Faustus kisses); The Chorus (The speaker who opens and closes the story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Doctor Faustus is Dr. Johann Georg Faust (a German alchemist, astrologer and magician) in real life.
Full title of the play is "The Tragical History of the Life and Death of Doctor Faustus."
Its first performance was in 1592, but was published in 1609. It is written in 5 acts.
Doctor Faustus is a talented German Scholar who was born of ordinary parents in Rhodes, Germany.
In the prologue, the chorus introduces the story of Doctor Faustus.
Doctor Faustus is compared to a Greek mythological character named Icarus in the prologue. Wagner is the servant of Dr. Faustus.
Before he turns to magic, he was considered to study logic, medicine, law and religion (Theology).
He learned everything he could learn, all of these things left him unsatisfied, so now he turns to magic.
A good and a bad angel arrive, representing Faustus's choice between Christian conscience and a path to damnation respectively. While the former advises him to leave off the pursuit of magic, the later tempts him for this.
From two fellow Scholars Valdes and Cornelius, Faustus learns the fundamental of the black arts.
Faustus summons Mephistopheles and ask him to appear in the shape of Franciscan Friar.
Faustus sells his soul, in exchange for 24 years of power with Mephistopheles as servant to his every whim.
Faustus signs the deal writing with his own blood. The word "homo fuge" (fly man) appears on his arm and Faustus is seized by his fear.
The good angel tells him to repent while the evil angel tells him to stick to his wicked ways.
Lucifer, the ruler of hell promises Dr. Faustus to show him hell.
Mephistopheles replies all questions of Dr. Faustus, except who made the world because he says that the answer to this question is against our kingdom.
Faustus explored the heavens and the earth from a chariot drawn by dragons, and is now flying to Rome, where the feast honouring St. Peter is about to be celebrated.
At Rome he makes himself invisible and plays a series of tricks. He disrupts the Pope's banquet by stealing food and boxing Pope's ears.
After this he travels through the courts of Europe with his fame spreading everywhere.
He is called upon by German Emperor Charles V, who asks Faustus to allow him to see Alexander the Great. Faustus impressed him by conjuring Alexander's image. Here Faustus also humiliates a knight name Benvolio. When Benvolio and his friend try to avenge the humiliation, Faustus asked his devils to hunt them and transform them so that the horns grow on their head.
Faustus then plays tricks on a horse - Courser. Faustus sold his own horse to him and asked not to take it to water but when horse - curser take it into the water to know the truth. It turns into a heap of straw.
Faustus is then invited to the court of Duke of Vanholt, where he performs various feats. There Faustus met all his earlier victims but sent them on their way.
When 24 years of deal came close, Faustus asked Mephistopheles to call Helen of Troy, the famous beauty of the ancient world.
An old man urges Faustus to repent but he drives him away.
On the final night before the expiration of the deal Faustus is overcome by fear and remorse, and at midnight a host of devils appear and carries his soul off to hell. Note - Necromancy means "The study of dead souls"
A 20th century theatre director Jerzy Grotowski produced Doctor Faustus for his theatre laboratory in Opole, Poland in 1963. The plot was reduced to single scene in which Faustus on his deathbed is arguing with his students. He also presented double Mephistopheles replacing good and evil angel.
"The reward of sin is death that is hard---if we say that we have no sin."
"Was this the face that launched the thousand ships".
"Come Helen come, make me immortal with a kiss".
Faustus masters lawful learning and then turns to magic.
He calls up Mephistophilis and signs away his soul in blood.
A Good Angel and an Evil Angel pull him two ways.
He wastes his years on shows, tricks, and the sight of Helen of Troy.
At the end he cannot repent, and devils carry him off.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Edward II

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1594 (Sort Year: 1594)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christopher Marlowe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: King Edward II loses his crown and his life because he loves Gaveston and neglects the realm.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The earliest surviving book is the 1594 edition. That book names Marlowe and says the play was acted in London by Pembroke's Men. It was printed after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward II (The king, whose love for his favourites costs him the throne); Piers Gaveston (Edward's first favourite, hated by the barons); Queen Isabella (Edward's neglected wife, who joins the rebellion); Mortimer (A noble who leads the revolt and is later executed); Edward III (The young king who restores order at the end)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Full title - "The Trouble some Reign and Lamentable death of Edward the Second, King of England, with the Tragical fall of Proud Mortimer."
There is a depiction of "Homosexual affection" between Edward II and Gavestone in this play. Frederic Boas elaborates the homosexual relation of Edward and Gavestone.
Marlow found the material of this play from Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles (1587).
The play was published in 1594 after the death of Marlow.
The play starts with the recall of Edward II's favourite Piers Gavestone from exile and ends with the execution of Mortimer Junior by Edward III for Edward II's murder.
When Edward II gains the throne he recalls Gavestone from exile. Gavestone plans to delight the king by entertaining him as "Music and poetry is his delight Therefore I'll have Italian masques by night…"
Upon Gavestone's re-entry into the country, Edward gives him titles, access to the royal treasury and guards to protect him.
Gavestone pleases king by Italian masques, music and poetry but got very less favour from king's nobles. Edward is forced to agree about reasons of Gavestone's exile and he banished Gavestone to Ireland.
Isabella of France, the Queen hopes for the favour of Gavestone, persuades Mortimer (who later becomes lover of the Queen) to argue Gavestone's recall, so that he can be easily killed.
The nobles Warwick and Lancester execute Gavestone and eventually Edward in turn executes them.
Edward seeks comfort with Spencer and his father.
Isabella takes Mortimer as her lover and travel to France in search of allies. She didn't get any help from France but Sir John of Hainault helps her.
Spenser and his father are executed and King Edward is taken to Kenilworth.
Edmund, Earl of Kent is arrested and executed by Mortimer for approaching the imprisoned Edward II.
Edmund was the brother of Edward II and Mortimer executed him saying that he is the threat to the throne.
King Edward II as a prisoner is taken to Berkeley Castle where he meets the luxuriously cruel Lightborn whose name is an anglicised version of 'Lucifer'.
Lightborn kills Edward II. Maltravers and Gurney witnesses this and Gurney killed Lightborn to keep him silent.
Edward III discovered the plot of Mortimer and his mother Isabella. Edward III orders Mortimer's death but Isabella pleads her son for Mortimer's life. But he refused.
The play ends with Mortimer's death, Isabella's imprisonment and Edward III taking the throne.
Note: Shakespeare's Richard II & III are based on Edward II of Marlow.
Edward recalls his favourite, Piers Gaveston, and angers the nobles.
The nobles force Gaveston into exile and later have him killed.
Edward takes a new favourite, Spencer, and defeats his enemies for a time.
Queen Isabella and Mortimer rebel, and Edward is forced to give up the crown.
Lightborn murders Edward in Berkeley Castle.
Young Edward III then punishes Mortimer.

items.title: "Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay" (1594) — Robert Greene

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1594 (Sort Year: 1594)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Greene

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic play about a prince's love and a magician's talking brass head.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is only the period start. The first printing is 1594. A Friar Bacon play was acted on 19 February 1592.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prince Edward (Son of Henry III, who loves Margaret and later marries Elinor); Margaret (The Fair Maid of Fressingfield, loved by Edward and by Lacy); Lacy (Earl of Lincoln and Edward's friend, who marries Margaret); Friar Bacon (An Oxford magician based on the real scholar Roger Bacon); Friar Bungay (A second magician who helps Bacon make the brass head); Miles (Bacon's comic servant, who fails to wake him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Orlando Furioso, based on Aristo's Orlando Furioso.
On attacking Shakespeare he used a term "Shake - scene" to refer the actor.
Green attacked Shakespeare as an "Upstart Crow" because at his end time Shakespeare had been an upstart actor contributing on Henry VI and King John. "An upstart crow beautified with our feathers" is a title quote from Groats-Worth of Wit.
Greene wrote "A looking Glass for London and England" in collaboration with Thomas Lodge.
The Comical History of Alphonsus, King of Aragon was also written by Greene in 1590.
Greene is most familiar to Shakespeare for his pamphlet "Groats Worth of Wit" which alludes to a line "O tigers heart wrapped in a women's hide" found in Shakespeare's Henry VI, part III (1623)
Prince Edward loves Margaret, the Fair Maid of Fressingfield.
He sends his friend Lacy to woo her, but Lacy and Margaret fall in love.
Edward rages, then forgives them, and marries Elinor of Castile.
Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay make a brass head that can speak.
The head says time is, time was, and time is past, then it breaks.
Bacon's servant Miles does not wake him, so the magic fails.
Two scholars see their fathers die in Bacon's glass and kill each other.
Bacon gives up magic.
Miles rides to hell on a devil's back.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Gorboduc

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1565 (Sort Year: 1565)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: King Gorboduc splits Britain between two sons, and the realm falls into murder and civil war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was acted in 1561 and first printed on 22 September 1565. The Whitehall show was on 18 January 1561 by the old calendar. Some books call that date 1562. A corrected edition in 1570 is titled Ferrex and Porrex.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gorboduc (King of ancient Britain who divides the kingdom while he is still alive); Ferrex (Elder son, who receives one half of the kingdom); Porrex (Younger son, who kills his brother); Videna (Queen and mother, who kills Porrex to avenge Ferrex); Eubulus (Wise adviser who warns against dividing the kingdom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gorboduc, a king in ancient Britain, gives half the land to each son.
The elder son is Ferrex.
The younger son is Porrex.
Bad advisers push the brothers to fear each other.
Porrex kills Ferrex.
Their mother, Videna, then kills Porrex.
The people kill the king and queen.
With no heir, the nobles start a long civil war.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hero and Leander

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1598 (Sort Year: 1598)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christopher Marlowe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished love poem in which Leander swims the Hellespont to reach the priestess Hero.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Marlowe died in 1593 with the poem unfinished. Two books appeared in 1598. One prints only Marlowe. The other adds Chapman's ending. Henry Petowe also wrote a different ending.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hero (A priestess of Venus who lives in a tower at Sestos); Leander (A young man of Abydos who swims to her each night); Neptune (The sea god who falls in love with Leander as he swims)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an epic poem by Marlow.
Hero and Leander is the Greek myth relating the story of Hero, a priestess of Aphrodite and Leander, a young man from Abydos.
Leander fell in love with Hero and would swim every night across Hellespont to be with her. Hero would light a lamp at the top of her tower to guide his way.
Hero allowed Leander to love her, but one stormy winter night the waves tossed Leander in the sea and the breezes blew out Hero's light; Leander lost his way and was drowned.
Hero saw his dead body and threw herself over the edge of the tower to her death, to be with him.
The poem remained unfinished but later completed by George Chapman in 1598.
There is a depiction of 'homosexual affection' between Leander and Neptune in the poem.
Shakespeare's 'Venus and Adonis' is based on Marlow's Hero and Leander.
Hero, a devotee of Venus, meets Leander at a festival.
Leander argues her out of her vow of chastity (a promise not to marry).
He swims the narrow sea.
Neptune mistakes him for the youth Ganymede.
Hero lets him into her tower, and the night ends in love.
Marlowe's part stops at dawn.
George Chapman later added an ending in which both die.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Idea

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1594 (Sort Year: 1594)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Michael Drayton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sonnet sequence addressed to Idea and revised by the poet for many years.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The sequence starts with Ideas Mirrour in 1594. The final form is in Poems (1619). The parting sonnet first appears in that 1619 book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A lover who claims he can leave Idea, then almost yields); Idea (The woman addressed in the sonnets, linked with Anne Goodere)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The first version, called Ideas Mirrour, was printed in 1594.
Drayton cut, rewrote, and added sonnets in later editions.
Idea is linked with Anne Goodere, daughter of the man who first supported him.
The 1619 collection Poems holds the final group of 64 sonnets.
Its best known poem is a sonnet of parting that nearly calls the love back.

items.title: "Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity" (1593) — Richard Hooker

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1593 (Sort Year: 1593)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Richard Hooker

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long prose defence of the Church of England, its worship, and its law.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Books 1 to 4 were published in 1593. Book 5 was published in 1597. Books 6 and 8 were printed in 1648. Book 7 was printed in 1662. Only Books 1 to 5 appeared in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Richard Hooker (The priest and author who argues the case for the English church)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Puritans had attacked the prayer book, the bishops, and the queen's church.
Hooker plans eight books in reply.
Book 1 explains kinds of law and says law has its seat in God.
Books 2 to 5 defend reason, church custom, and English public worship.
He died before the last books were finished, so they were printed later.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Rosalynde

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1590 (Sort Year: 1590)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Lodge

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A pastoral romance (a country love story) that gave Shakespeare the plot of As You Like It.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period start, not the print year. The first edition appeared in 1590.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rosader (Youngest son of Sir John, cheated by his brother and later a lover); Saladyne (Eldest brother, who steals the inheritance and is later reformed); Rosalynde (Daughter of the banished king, disguised as the page Ganymede); Alinda (Torismond's daughter, who flees with Rosalynde under the name Aliena); Gerismond (Rightful king of France, living as an outlaw in the Forest of Arden); Adam Spencer (Old servant who escapes with Rosader)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sir John of Bordeaux dies and leaves land to his three sons.
The eldest, Saladyne, steals the share of the youngest, Rosader.
Rosader wins a wrestling match and meets Rosalynde at court.
King Torismond has banished his brother Gerismond to the forest.
Rosalynde and Alinda flee to Arden as Ganymede and Aliena.
Rosader and the old servant Adam Spencer also reach the forest.
Ganymede pretends to be Rosalynde and tests Rosader's love.
The brothers make peace, the true king returns, and the lovers marry.

items.title: "Summer’s Last Will and Testament" (1600) — Thomas Nashe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Summer’s Last Will and Testament

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1600 (Sort Year: 1600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Nashe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Dying Summer hears his servants' accounts, then leaves his crown to Autumn.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Scholars place the show at Croydon Palace in autumn 1592, while plague closed the London theatres. Archbishop John Whitgift was the host. It was entered in the Stationers' Register on 28 October 1600 and printed that year. The database lists this play under fiction. It is drama.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Will Summers (Henry VIII's jester, who presents the play and jokes about it.); Summer (The dying king of the year, who calls his servants to account.); Autumn (The season that receives Summer's crown.); Ver (The figure of spring among the seasons.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Will Summers, the old court jester, introduces the show and mocks it.
Summer is old and ready to make his will.
Spring, Autumn, Winter, and other servants give their accounts.
Songs, dances, and harvest figures fill the show.
A plague lyric says that beauty and joy do not last.
Summer passes his crown to Autumn.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Tamburlaine

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1590 (Sort Year: 1590)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christopher Marlowe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Scythian shepherd conquers kings by speech and war, then dies still hungering for more.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Part 1 was on stage in 1587. Both parts were printed together in 1590, with no author name on that first book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tamburlaine (A shepherd who becomes a world conqueror); Zenocrate (The captive princess who becomes his wife); Bajazeth (The Turkish emperor whom Tamburlaine cages and mocks)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a play in two parts based on the life of Central Asian emperor, Timur.
The play was entered into the Stationer's Register in 1590. Both parts were published together in a single black letter Octavo in 1590 by printer Richard Jones.
Tamburlaine, a shepherd, defeats the Persian king and takes the crown.
He wins Zenocrate and cages the Turkish emperor Bajazeth.
Part 1 ends in marriage and triumph.
In Part 2, Zenocrate dies, and his sons disappoint him.
He burns holy books and dies of sickness, still calling himself the scourge of God.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Defence of Poesy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1595 (Sort Year: 1595)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Philip Sidney

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical treatise arguing that poetry teaches virtue better than history or philosophy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: This is criticism. Sidney wrote it before 1583, partly after Stephen Gosson's School of Abuse (1579). It was printed in 1595, after his death. Ponsonby's title is The Defence of Poesie. The same text also appeared as An Apology for Poetry. See the next entry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philip Sidney (The author and speaker of the defence)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sidney answers old charges that poetry is a waste of time and a mother of lies.
He defines poetry as an art of imitation that makes a golden world.
The poet invents examples that move readers to act well.
He ranks heroical poetry (epic) as the highest kind.
He ends by urging England to take poetry seriously.
The book came out after he died.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Faerie Queene

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1590 (Books 1-3), 1596 (Books 4-6) (Sort Year: 1590)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edmund Spenser

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished epic in which knights act out moral virtues for Queen Elizabeth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Books 1 to 3 were printed in 1590. Books 4 to 6 were printed in 1596. The poem was planned in twelve books and left unfinished.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gloriana (The fairy queen, a figure for Queen Elizabeth I); Prince Arthur (A knight who seeks Gloriana and helps the other heroes); Red Cross Knight (The knight of holiness in Book 1, later named Saint George); Una (A pure lady who stands for truth and the true church); Duessa (A false beauty who stands for deceit); Britomart (The woman knight of chastity in Book 3)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the epic poem of Spenser. It is written in Spenserian stanza (abab bcbc c). All the books are based on 'King Arthur'.
The first three books were published in 1590 and second set of three books were published in 1596. Spenser states that; "the aim behind the Faerie Queene was to- Fashion a gentleman or noble person in virtuous and gentle discipline".
Actually Spenser had planned to write 24 books but it remained unfinished.
The introductory letter of Faerie Queene was written to Walter Raleigh.
Dryden commented on it for its 'Lack of Unity.'
It is an allegorical epic poem in which we can find the praise of Queen Elizabeth as Gloriana.
Each book represents a virtue of a knight.
Spenser called this epic as "a dark conceit."
The seventh book was incomplete which deals with the subject of mutability represent the virtue of Constancy.
The six books represents the following virtues of the knights: i)
Prince Arthur searches for Gloriana, the fairy queen, who stands for Elizabeth.
Book 1 follows the Red Cross Knight, the knight of holiness, and Una, who stands for truth.
Book 2 follows Guyon, the knight of temperance (self control).
Book 3 follows Britomart, a woman knight of chastity (faithful love).
Books 4 to 6 treat friendship, justice, and courtesy.
The poem then breaks off.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Jew of Malta

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1633 (Sort Year: 1633)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christopher Marlowe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The rich Jew Barabas takes revenge on Malta's rulers and dies in his own boiling trap.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was entered for printing in 1594, but the earliest surviving book is the 1633 quarto. That book adds prologues by Thomas Heywood. The 1633 date is long after Marlowe's death in 1593.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Barabas (A rich Jewish merchant whose greed and revenge drive the plot); Abigail (His daughter, who becomes a nun and is poisoned); Ferneze (The Christian governor of Malta); Ithamore (A slave who helps Barabas and then turns on him); Machiavel (The prologue speaker, a stage figure of cunning policy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play opens with a prologue narrated by Machevill, a caricature of the author Machiavelli. Machevill explains that he is presenting the 'Tragedy of a Jew' who has become rich by following Machiavelli's teachings.
Barabas, a Christian hating merchant of Malta receives in his country house a party of merchants who report the arrival of several vessels laden with wealth from the East. At the same time three Jews arrived to announce for an important meeting at the senate with Governor Ferneze.
The point of the meeting was that, the Turkish master of Malta demanded the overdue payment which Turkish Seignior purposely lets the payment lapse over a period of years, so that the Maltese will have choice of either payment or surrender.
The Christian governor of the island, attempting to collect the tribute (Overdue payment) in a month. He gave a judicial decision that the Jews will have to give over half of their estates or become Christian.
All the Jewish community except Barabas agreed to the decree of the Governor and seizes all Barabas's wealth as punishment and Jews' house were turned into Christian convent.
Barabas vows to take revenge from the governor.
Barabas, to avoid complete ruin, purposely not reported the part of his treasure hidden in the foundation of his house.
He persuaded his daughter Abigail, to pretend that she has converted to Christianity so that she might enter the convent to recover the treasure.
Abigail does her work dutifully and throws the money bag out of the window to her waiting father.
Martin De Bosco, vice admiral of Spain sells one of his slaves to Barabas. The slave is an Arabian named Ithamore.
He asks his daughter Abigail to show favour to the invited two young men to his house, one is Don Lodowick, the governor's son and Don Mathias. Barabas wanted Abigail to be betrothed to Lodowick.
Lodowick had heard about Abigail's beauty from his friend Mathais, so he was duped by Barabas thinking Abigail will marry him.
At the end of second act these two young men vow revenge on each other in order to woo Abigail.
Barabas send a forged letter to Mathais through Ithamore, supposedly from Lodowick, challenging him for a dual.
In act III, Bellamira and her pimp Pillia Borza both the prostitutes plan to steal some of Barabas' gold.
Ithamore fell in love with Bellamira.
Lodowick and Mathais killed each other in the dual.
Ferneze the governor and his wife Katherine vows revenge to Barabas.
Ithamore tells Abigail about her father's role in the young man's death.
Abigail was enraged from his father's acts; she entered into the convent to become a nun with the help of a Dominician friar Jacomo.
Barabas kills all the nuns of the convent by poisoning them in the rice, as he was enraged by the act of her daughter.
Ferneze meets Turks and explains that he will not pay the required tribute. The Turks leave warning that Calymath, their leader will attack the island.
Jacomo and another Friar Bernardine are despaired about death of all nuns. Abigail who is also close to death tells the Friars about her father's role in Mathias's and Lodowick's death.
Barabas and Ithamore were delighted at the Nun's death. He is confronted by Jacomo and Bernardine and realized that Abigail has confessed his crimes to these Friars.
In order to distract the Friars, Barabas pretends to convert to Christianity. Jacomo and Bernardine fights to get the Jew in their own religious houses.
Barabas tricks Bernardine to come to his home. Ithamore strangles (killed by choking throat) Bernardine and Barabas framed Jacomo for the crime.
Ithamore confesses his master's crime to Bellamira and she decides to report this matter to the Governor. Barabas is maddened by Ithamore's treachery. He disguised as a French Lute Player and poisoned all three conspirators by using a poisoned flower (Bellamira, Pillia Borza & Ithamore).
In the final act when Ferneze came to know about Barabas' crime. Barabas fakes his own death and escapes to find Calymath.
Malta is captured by the Turkish forces and Barabas is made governor. Calymath prepares to leave.
Fearing his own life, Barabas tells Ferneze that he will free Malta from Turkish rule and kill Calymath in exchange for a large amount of money.
Ferneze agrees and Barabas invites Calymath to a feast at his home. When Calymath arrives, Ferneze prevents Barabas from killing him.
Barabas dies in a Cauldron that he had prepared for killing Calymath.
Ferneze told Calymath that he will be a prisoner in Malta until the Ottoman emperor agrees to free the Island.
Note: This play has been considered to have a major influence on Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venice".
Important Quote: "I count religion but a childish toy and hold there is no sin but ignorance" - by Machevill.
A speaker called Machiavel opens the play and praises cunning policy.
The governor seizes Barabas's wealth to pay tribute to the Turks.
Barabas makes his daughter Abigail help him recover hidden gold.
He poisons, tricks, and betrays until he becomes governor himself.
His last trap, a boiling cauldron, kills him instead of the Turkish prince.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Old Wives’ Tale

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1595 (Sort Year: 1595)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Peele

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old woman tells a magic tale, and the tale is acted out with songs and jokes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: John Danter printed the play in 1595. The Queen's Men (the queen's acting company) had played it. The exact first performance year is not certain.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Madge (The old wife who starts the tale by the fire); Sacrapant (The magician who keeps the princess captive); Erestus (The old man at the cross who speaks in riddles); Huanebango (A boastful knight who mocks the style of romance heroes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Three lost serving boys take shelter with Clunch and his wife Madge.
Madge begins a bedtime story, and the story comes alive on stage.
A magician named Sacrapant holds a princess captive.
A boastful knight, Huanebango, and two brothers try to free her.
Riddles, songs, and a magic well break the spell.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Shepheardes Calender

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1579 (Sort Year: 1579)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edmund Spenser

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twelve shepherd poems, one for each month, about love, the church, and poetry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both opened sources date the first printing to 1579. It was entered in the Stationers' Register in December 1579.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Colin Clout (The sad shepherd poet, a figure for Spenser); Hobbinol (Colin's friend, often linked with Gabriel Harvey); Eliza (The shepherdess praised in April, a figure for the queen)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is dedicated to Philip Sidney and signed with the name Immerito.
Colin Clout, a figure for Spenser, loves Rosalind and is refused.
Each month is a separate eclogue (a short shepherd poem), often a debate or a song.
April praises Eliza, a figure for the queen.
Other months debate church abuses.
A commentator called E.K. adds notes after the poems.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Spanish Tragedy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1592 (Sort Year: 1592)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Kyd

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hieronimo avenges his murdered son through a court play in which the killers really die.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is Kyd's baptism year, not the play. The Stationers' Register entry is 6 October 1592, and the surviving quarto is from that year. Early editions are anonymous. A 1602 edition adds extra passages. Scholars often guess a first performance about 1587, but the night is not recorded.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hieronimo (Knight Marshal of Spain, who goes mad and avenges his son); Horatio (Hieronimo's son, murdered in the garden); Bel Imperia (A Spanish princess who loves Horatio and joins the revenge); Lorenzo (Bel imperia's brother, who plans Horatio's murder); Balthazar (Prince of Portugal, who helps kill Horatio); Ghost of Andrea (A dead Spanish courtier who wants revenge); Revenge (A chorus figure who promises that justice will come)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The ghost of Andrea and the figure Revenge watch the whole play.
Balthazar of Portugal has killed Andrea, and Horatio has captured Balthazar.
Bel Imperia loves Horatio.
Lorenzo and Balthazar hang Horatio in the garden.
Hieronimo, Horatio's father, learns the killers' names and is refused justice.
In the play Soliman and Perseda he and Bel Imperia stab the murderers, then die.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Unfortunate Traveller

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1594 (Sort Year: 1594)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Nashe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jack Wilton, a clever rogue, travels through Europe and tells wild, cruel adventures.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The book was printed in 1594 by Thomas Scarlet for Cuthbert Burby. A corrected edition came out the same year. The database unit calls it poetry. That is wrong. It is prose fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jack Wilton (The rogue who narrates his travels and lives by tricks.); Earl of Surrey (The poet who travels with Jack and fights for his lady Geraldine.); Diamante (The woman who becomes Jack's companion and later his wife.); Pietro Aretino (The Italian satirist who helps free Jack and Surrey.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a picaresque novel set during reign of Henry VIII of England.
Jack Wilton is a page serving in the army of King Henry VIII of England when his adventures begin.
Jack tries of his subservience to the captain and persuades the officer that the best means of getting ahead in the army is to turn spy and seek valuable information to the King.
'Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey' functions as a sustained travel partner of Jack Wilton and both journeys to Italy to fulfill the Earl's pledge to defend the honour of his beloved Geraldine in a tournament.
At the end of the play Jack and his newly wed Diamant flee out of "the Sodom of Italy" back toward the English Encampment in France where the story first began.
Quote: "This is the fault that hath called me hither. No true Italian but will honour me for it. Revenge is the glory of arms and the highest performance of Valour." - Oration by Cutwolfe.
Jack cheats soldiers and officers in an English army camp.
He sees the killing of Anabaptists (a radical religious group) at Munster.
He travels with the Earl of Surrey and meets Erasmus and Thomas More.
In Italy the two men swap names and fall into crime and prison.
Jack joins Diamante, sees terrible violence in Rome, and escapes death.
After a public revenge killing in Bologna, he and Diamante leave Italy.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Euphues

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1578 (Sort Year: 1578)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lyly

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose romance about a clever young man whose wit fails him in love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1578 is correct. It was printed in London for Gabriel Cawood. The sequel, Euphues and His England, is a different book from 1580.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Euphues (A witty young man of Athens who learns the limits of cleverness); Philautus (His friend in Naples); Lucilla (The woman who comes between the two friends)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Euphues leaves Athens for Naples and befriends a man named Philautus.
He falls in love with Lucilla, who had been promised to Philautus.
Lucilla leaves both men, and the friendship breaks.
Euphues goes back to Athens and turns from love to study.
The tale keeps pausing for letters on wit, women, and education.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pandosto

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1588 (Sort Year: 1588)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Greene

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose romance of jealousy, a lost daughter, and the slow work of time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1588 is right for the first printing. The database calls this work drama, but it is a prose romance. A 1607 edition is titled Dorastus and Fawnia.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pandosto (King of Bohemia, destroyed by groundless jealousy); Bellaria (His loyal wife, who dies after the false charge); Egistus (King of Sicilia and Pandosto's old friend); Fawnia (Their daughter, set adrift and raised by a shepherd); Dorastus (Prince of Sicilia, who loves Fawnia and flees with her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pandosto, King of Bohemia, falsely accuses his wife Bellaria.
He thinks she loves his friend Egistus, King of Sicilia.
His son and his wife die, and he sets the baby Fawnia adrift.
A shepherd in Sicilia raises Fawnia.
Prince Dorastus loves her, and they flee to Bohemia.
Pandosto, not knowing her, falls in love with his own daughter.
When the truth appears, he kills himself in grief.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Arcadia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1590, composite edition 1593 (Sort Year: 1590)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Philip Sidney

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A pastoral romance of princes, disguises, love, and war, left unfinished and later patched together.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poetry Foundation dates the New Arcadia book to 1590. It dates the Old Arcadia to about 1581. Wikipedia dates Greville's unfinished text to 1590 and Mary's composite book to 1593. A 1621 edition added a bridge by William Alexander. The work is prose romance, not drama.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pyrocles (A prince who disguises himself as the Amazon Zelmane to woo Philoclea); Musidorus (His cousin, who disguises himself as a shepherd to woo Pamela); Philoclea (The younger princess, loved by Pyrocles); Pamela (The elder princess, loved by Musidorus); Basilius (The duke who hides his family in the country because of an oracle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sidney asserted that he wrote it to entertain his sister Mary Herbert, the countess of Pembroke. It is a romance in Prose.
The early version of Arcadia is called "Old Arcadia". He himself edited it and the new version is called "New Arcadia".
Later the "New Arcadia" was edited by Fulke Greville, Mathew Gwinne and John Florio and published in bigger form to Old Arcadia in 1590.
In 1593, Mary Herbert, herself published an edition of Arcadia called - "The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia"
This work is often called 'tragicomic' in 5 acts. It contains several eclogues.
Book I is about Basilius, Duke of Arcadia. His wife is Gynecia and two attractive daughters Pamela and Philoclea. His daughters are stolen by undesirable suitors and are cuckolded by his wife.
Samuel Richardson has adopted the name of his novel Pamela from here.
Sidney first wrote the Old Arcadia about 1580, in five books, while staying with his sister.
Two princes, Musidorus and Pyrocles, disguise themselves to woo Pamela and Philoclea.
He then rewrote the story as the New Arcadia, with more battles and nested tales.
The revision breaks off in a fight.
Fulke Greville printed that unfinished text in 1590.
In 1593 his sister Mary published a composite book, joining the new opening to the old ending.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Astrophil and Stella

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1591, authorised 1598 (Sort Year: 1591)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Philip Sidney

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sequence of 108 sonnets and 11 songs in which Astrophil loves the married Stella.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and the Poetry Foundation agree on 1591. The poems were written in the early 1580s. The 1591 book was apparently pirated. The authorised text came in 1598, inside the Arcadia folio.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Astrophil (The star lover, the speaking poet of the sequence); Stella (The star he loves, linked with Penelope Devereux, Lady Rich)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Astrophil tries to write about love and is told to look in his heart.
He praises Stella, suffers, hopes, and despairs from poem to poem.
Stella is linked with Penelope Devereux, later Lady Rich.
The sequence was written in the early 1580s and passed about in manuscript.
A pirated book appeared in 1591. An authorised text came in 1598.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Endymion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1591 (Sort Year: 1591)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lyly

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A court comedy in which a man sleeps for years out of love for the moon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says printed 1591, which is right. Britannica and later accounts place the court performance in 1588. Do not treat 1588 and 1591 as the same event.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Endymion (A courtier who loves Cynthia and sleeps for many years); Cynthia (The moon goddess, standing for Queen Elizabeth); Tellus (A woman jealous of Endymion's love for Cynthia); Eumenides (Endymion's loyal friend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a play by Lyly. Endymion is in love with Goddess of Moon, Cynthia. They never got married because Cynthia was a Goddess.
The play provides a vivid example of the cult of flattery in the royal court of Elizabeth.
It has been called, "without doubt, the boldest in conception and the most beautiful in execution of all Lyly's plays".
Endymion is finally awakened of a kiss by Cynthia. Note: Endymion is also written by Keats.
It starts with "A thing of beauty is a joy forever."
Endymion was a handsome, young shepherd prince loved by the moon goddess Selene.
Endymion loves Cynthia, the moon, a figure of Queen Elizabeth.
Tellus, a jealous woman, has him cast into a long sleep.
Faithful friends seek a cure while years pass.
A kiss from Cynthia wakes him.
He accepts a life of service, and the court is pardoned and paired off.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Gallathea

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1592 (Sort Year: 1592)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Lyly

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two girls, disguised as boys, fall in love and refuse to part.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database printing date, 1592, is correct. Britannica places the performance between 1585 and 1588. Wikipedia narrows the likely court night to the 1587 to 1588 season. The spelling Galatea is also used.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gallathea (A girl disguised as a boy who loves Phillida); Phillida (A girl disguised as a boy who loves Gallathea); Neptune (The sea god who demands that a beautiful girl be sacrificed); Venus (Goddess of love, who allows the match); Diana (Goddess who tells the girls to give up their love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
5. Midas (1592) and 6. Mother Bombie (1594)
Love's Metamorphosis was left out among the six comedies.
Lyly made a deep influence on Shakespeare. Love's metamorphosis has deep influence on Shakespeare's Love's Labour lost.
Gallathea of Lyly has influence on Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream.
The proverb "All is fair in Love and War" has been attributed to "Eupheus".
Francis Meres places him among "The best for comedy."
Ben Jonson named Lyly among these foremost rivals who were 'Outshone and Out sung' by Shakespeare.
The Maid's Metamorphosis is a late Elizabethan stage play, a pastoral first published in 1600. The play, "a comedy of considerable merit," was published anonymously, and its authorship has been a long-standing point of dispute among scholars although attributed to Lyly.
Modern commentators have praised this play as "Harmonious Variety' and "Allegorical dramaturgy."
Neptune demands the sacrifice of the fairest unmarried girl.
Two fathers disguise their daughters, Gallathea and Phillida, as boys.
The girls meet in the woods and fall in love.
Each had thought the other was a boy.
Venus promises that one of them will be changed so they can marry.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Venus and Adonis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1593 (Quarto) (Sort Year: 1593)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The goddess of love woos a handsome young hunter who rejects her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives 1593, which matches the first quarto printing. Shakespeare called it the first heir of his invention.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Venus (The Roman goddess of love and beauty); Adonis (A handsome young hunter who resists Venus)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Venus falls passionately in love with the youthful hunter Adonis.
She begs him for kisses, but he prefers hunting.
Adonis warns her that he intends to hunt a wild boar.
The boar attacks and kills Adonis in the woods.
Venus grieves deeply, and the blood of Adonis turns into an anemone flower.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Romeo and Juliet

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1597 (Quarto 1), 1599 (Quarto 2), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1597)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two young lovers from feuding families marry in secret and die together.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1594-1596 and Quarto 1597. Quarto 1 was a bad quarto (pirated memorial reconstruction). Quarto 2 was the true authorised edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Romeo (The son of Montague who loves Juliet); Juliet (The thirteen-year-old daughter of Capulet); Friar Laurence (A Franciscan friar who marries the lovers); Mercutio (Romeo's witty friend and kinsman to the Prince); Tybalt (Juliet's hot-tempered cousin slain by Romeo)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Montague and Capulet families wage an ancient feud in Verona.
Romeo Montague meets Juliet Capulet at a masked ball and they fall in love.
Friar Laurence marries the young pair secretly, hoping to reconcile the families.
Tybalt kills Mercutio, so Romeo slays Tybalt and is banished from Verona.
Juliet takes a sleeping potion to avoid marrying Paris, but Romeo believes she is truly dead.
Romeo drinks poison in her tomb, and Juliet awakens and stabs herself with his dagger.

items.title: "A Midsummer Night’s Dream" (1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)) — William Shakespeare

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Midsummer Night’s Dream

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four Athenian lovers and amateur actors encounter mischievous fairies in an enchanted forest.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1595-1596 and Quarto 1600, which is correct. Francis Meres mentioned it in 1598.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Puck (Robin Goodfellow) (Oberon's mischievous fairy servant); Oberon (King of the fairies); Titania (Queen of the fairies); Nick Bottom (A weaver transformed into a donkey); Theseus (Duke of Athens celebrating his marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hermia and Lysander flee to the woods to escape an arranged marriage, followed by Demetrius and Helena.
Fairy king Oberon and queen Titania feud over a changeling boy.
Puck mistakenly smears love juice on Lysander and Demetrius, turning their affections upside down.
Puck transforms the weaver Bottom into a donkey, and enchanted Titania falls in love with him.
Oberon restores order with a counter charm, and three happy couples celebrate a triple wedding.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Amoretti

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1595 (Sort Year: 1595)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edmund Spenser

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eighty nine sonnets about Spenser's courtship of Elizabeth Boyle, ending in marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Amoretti was printed with Epithalamion in 1595, after his marriage to Elizabeth Boyle in 1594.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The lover poet (The speaker, linked with Spenser himself); Elizabeth Boyle (The lady of the sonnets, whom Spenser married in 1594)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It was published by William Ponsonby in volume entitled "Amoretti and Epithalamion."
Amoretti is an Italian word which means 'little love gift' or 'little love poems.'
It is a sequence of 89 sonnets dedicated to his second wife Elizabeth Boyle.
In the first four lines the author compares himself to a book that is read by his love Elizabeth.
He hopes that Elizabeth will hold his poems in her 'Lily white hands.'
Rhyme scheme of the Sonnet - abab bcbc cdcd ee.
This Sonnet cycle ends with a set of stanzas returning to the poems title character 'Cupid.' The first set of stanza described how 'Cupid' led the speaker into Harem when he was young. Cupid causes speaker to draw his attention towards honey and when speaker reached to fetch it he was stung by bees and Cupid flew away.
The speaker praises a lady and also complains that she is proud.
The sequence follows a real courtship, unlike many sonnets of hopeless love.
Sonnet 67 shows the lady caught, like a deer that chooses to be won.
Sonnet 75 says his verse will keep her name alive after the waves wash it away.
The sonnets lead into the wedding song Epithalamion in the same book.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Epithalamion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1595 (Sort Year: 1595)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edmund Spenser

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wedding song for Spenser's marriage to Elizabeth Boyle, moving through one whole day.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was printed with Amoretti in 1595. The wedding it celebrates took place in 1594.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The bridegroom (The speaker, Spenser on his wedding day); Elizabeth Boyle (The bride praised through the hours of the day)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It was written by Spenser on his wedding with Elizabeth Boyle in 1594 but published in 1595. It is also called Nuptial Song.
It is an ode written to his bride Elizabeth Boyle.
When published by William Ponsonby, both works were included in the volume and Epithalamion and Amoretti were published together in 1595.
This song, actually sung by choirs of young men and women who accompanied the bride and groom from the bride's parents' house to her husband's family house where they would spend the wedding night. The Latin word Thalamos means 'bridal chamber.' The setting is Ireland. The poem contains 365 lines. He invokes 'Muses' at the beginning of the poem.
The Ode consists of 24 stanzas, each stanza contains 18 lines and each stanza corresponds to an hour of midsummer's day. 5.
The bridegroom calls the muses (goddesses of the arts) to wake his bride.
The poem follows the hours from dawn to the church and then to night.
Nymphs, boys, and the town join the procession.
Night brings prayers for children and for a quiet home.
The last stanza says the song itself will be a lasting monument.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Henry IV, Part 1

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1598 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1598)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Prince Hal leaves tavern life to help his royal father crush a rebellion.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1596-1597 and Quarto 1598, which is correct. Falstaff was originally named Sir John Oldcastle.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prince Hal (The Prince of Wales who matures into a heroic leader); Sir John Falstaff (A fat, witty, boastful, and cowardly knight); King Henry IV (The troubled king of England); Hotspur (Henry Percy) (A courageous but reckless rebel soldier)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King Henry IV faces an armed rebellion led by the fiery noble Hotspur.
Prince Hal spends his youth carousing in Eastcheap with the fat rascal Sir John Falstaff.
Hal vows to his father that he will cast off bad company and prove his royal worth.
At the Battle of Shrewsbury, Hal saves his father's life and kills Hotspur in single combat.
Falstaff dishonestly takes credit for Hotspur's defeat, but Hal permits his friend's boast.

items.title: "The Merchant of Venice" (1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)) — William Shakespeare

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Merchant of Venice

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A merchant pledges a pound of his own flesh to help his friend win an heiress.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1596-1598 and Quarto 1600, which is correct. Registered in July 1598.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Shylock (A bitter Jewish moneylender seeking revenge against Antonio); Portia (A clever and wealthy heiress of Belmont disguised as a lawyer); Antonio (The merchant of Venice who pledges his flesh for his friend); Bassanio (Antonio's dear friend who wins Portia through the casket trial)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bassanio seeks money to woo the wealthy heiress Portia in Belmont.
Antonio borrows three thousand ducats from Shylock, a Jewish moneylender.
Shylock demands a pound of Antonio's flesh as penalty if the loan is defaulted.
Antonio's merchant fleet is reported wrecked, and Shylock demands justice in court.
Portia disguises herself as a young lawyer and defeats Shylock by warning against spilling blood.
Shylock is stripped of half his property and forced to become Christian.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Essays

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1597, enlarged 1612 and 1625 (Sort Year: 1597)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Bacon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short essays of practical advice, growing from ten pieces in 1597 to fifty eight in 1625.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first book has 10 essays. The second has 38. The third has 58. Essays begin under Elizabeth and continue under James.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
I Edition (1595) - 10 essays were published including "Christian Meditations" and "Of the Colours of Good and Evil".
II Edition (1612) - It consisted 38 essays including "Of Death", "Of Religion", "Of Life", "Of Nobility of Dispatch", "Of Friendship", "Of Ambition", "Of Young Men and Age", "Of Beauty", "Of Nature in Men", "Of Custom and Education", "Of Fortune", "Of Vain Glory", "Of Praise", etc.
III Edition (1625) - It consists of 58 essays including "Of Truth", "Of Revenge", "Of Adversity", "Of Simulation and Dissimulation", "Of Envy", "Of Boldness", "Of Travel", "Of Delays", "Of Innovation", "Of Suspicion", "Of Plantation", "Of Prophecies", etc.
Full Title: - "Essayes: Religious Meditation Places of Perswasion and Disswasion. Seene and Allowed"
The 1597 book holds ten essays, including Of Studies.
Each essay turns one topic around and weighs one view against another.
