The 1612 book expands the set to thirty eight essays.
The 1625 book, Essayes or Counsels, Civill and Morall, holds fifty eight.
Famous pieces include Of Truth, Of Marriage and Single Life, and Of Revenge.

items.title: "Every Man in His Humour" (1601, revised in the 1616 folio) — Ben Jonson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Every Man in His Humour

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1601, revised in the 1616 folio (Sort Year: 1601)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A London comedy in which jealous, boastful, and foolish people are cured by a witty plot.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Lord Chamberlain's Men acted it in 1598. Shakespeare was in the cast. The first quarto is 1601, set in Florence. The 1616 folio revises the play and sets it in London.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Knowell (An old gentleman who tries to watch his son); Brainworm (The clever servant who runs the tricks); Kitely (A merchant tortured by jealousy); Bobadill (A boastful soldier who is really a coward); Justice Clement (The magistrate who sorts out the fools at the end)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Old Knowell spies on his son, but the servant Brainworm fools him.
The merchant Kitely is sick with jealousy about his wife.
Bobadill the braggart soldier and the two gulls add noise and lies.
Justice Clement hears every quarrel and shows that each fool is ruled by a humour.
The 1616 version changes the setting from Florence to London and gives the people English names.

items.title: "Much Ado About Nothing" (1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio)) — William Shakespeare

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Much Ado About Nothing

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1600 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two clever wits trade insults into romance while a villain falsely slanders an innocent bride.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1598-1599 and Quarto 1600, which is correct. Actor Will Kemp played Dogberry before 1599.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Beatrice (Leonato's sharp-tongued, witty niece); Benedick (A proud gentleman who vows to remain a bachelor); Hero (Leonato's sweet daughter who is falsely slandered); Claudio (A young lord who falsely accuses Hero); Dogberry (The bumbling master constable who mixes up words)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Beatrice and Benedick fight a merry war of wit and vow never to wed.
Their friends stage fake conversations to trick each into confessing love.
Hero and Claudio prepare to marry, but wicked Don John frames Hero as impure.
Claudio rejects Hero at the wedding, and she faints away and is reported dead.
The foolish constable Dogberry discovers Don John's deceit and clears Hero.
Hero and Claudio marry, and Beatrice and Benedick joyfully confess their mutual love.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Julius Caesar

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Roman conspirators assassinate Julius Caesar to save the republic, causing civil war and personal ruin.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1599 and First Folio 1623, which is correct. No early quarto was printed.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marcus Brutus (An honourable Roman senator who murders his friend Caesar for Rome); Julius Caesar (The powerful Roman dictator assassinated by the senate); Mark Antony (Caesar's devoted ally and skilled orator); Cassius (The envious senator who designs the conspiracy against Caesar)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Senators fear that the popular hero Julius Caesar will accept a crown as king.
Cassius persuades the honourable Brutus to join a plot against Caesar.
The conspirators murder Caesar in the Senate on the Ides of March (15 March).
Mark Antony delivers an emotional funeral speech that incites the Roman crowd to riot.
Antony and Octavius defeat Brutus and Cassius at the Battle of Philippi, where both conspirators kill themselves.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hamlet

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1603 (Quarto 1), 1604/1605 (Quarto 2), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1603)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Prince of Denmark plots revenge against his uncle for poisoning his royal father.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1603. Composed c. 1599-1601. Quarto 1 (1603) was a short bad quarto. Quarto 2 (1604) was the good full edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prince Hamlet (The philosophical, brooding Prince of Denmark); Claudius (Hamlet's murderous uncle who took the crown); Gertrude (Queen of Denmark and Hamlet's mother); Ophelia (Polonius's gentle daughter who drowns in grief); Horatio (Hamlet's loyal and steadfast friend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The ghost of King Hamlet appears and informs Prince Hamlet that his brother Claudius murdered him.
Claudius has claimed the throne and hastily wed Hamlet's grieving mother Gertrude.
Hamlet feigns madness while arranging a play to verify Claudius's guilt.
Claudius reacts with terror to the staged murder, confirming his crime.
Hamlet accidentally stabs Polonius behind a curtain, driving Ophelia insane with sorrow.
In a poisoned fencing match, Laertes, Gertrude, Claudius, and Hamlet are all killed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Old Fortunatus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1600 (Sort Year: 1600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Dekker

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A beggar chooses endless gold, and his sons waste the magic gifts and die.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Dekker wrote it in 1599 for the Admiral's Men (a London acting company). A court performance followed on 27 December 1599.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fortunatus (The poor man who chooses endless gold); Fortune (The goddess who gives the purse and later takes it back); Andelocia (The reckless son who wastes the purse and the hat); Ampedo (The cautious son who burns the wishing hat)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The goddess Fortune offers the beggar Fortunatus a choice of gifts.
He chooses riches and receives a purse that never runs empty.
He also steals a hat that can carry the wearer anywhere.
His sons Andelocia and Ampedo inherit the gifts and waste them.
Both sons die, Fortune takes the purse back, and the play warns against greed.

items.title: "A Chaste Maid in Cheapside" (1630) — Thomas Middleton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1630 (Sort Year: 1630)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Middleton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A London comedy about Moll, who escapes a bad match and seems to die before she weds.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was written and acted about 1613. The quarto (a small printed book) came out in 1630. Francis Constable published it. Do not use 1630 as the year of the first acting.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Moll Yellowhammer (The goldsmith's daughter who refuses the husband her father chose.); Touchwood Junior (The poor young man Moll loves and finally marries.); Sir Walter Whorehound (The greedy knight who wants Moll's money and keeps mistresses.); Allwit (A husband who is paid to accept his wife's lover. His name flips wittol (a husband who accepts that lover).)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Moll Yellowhammer loves Touchwood Junior, but her father wants Sir Walter Whorehound.
Sir Walter also keeps a mistress, and the husband Allwit accepts this for money.
He promises Moll's brother Tim a landed niece who is really another mistress.
Touchwood Senior helps the childless Kix couple, and Sir Walter loses his hoped fortune.
Moll is caught while fleeing and seems to fall ill.
She and Touchwood Junior pretend to die.
They rise from their coffins at the funeral and marry.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Horatian Ode

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1681 (Sort Year: 1681)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Andrew Marvell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A political poem on Cromwell's return from Ireland and the death of Charles I.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written soon after Cromwell left Ireland in May 1650. The database shows only the Jacobean span. Most copies of the 1681 book removed this poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A public voice weighing Cromwell's power and the king's death); Oliver Cromwell (The general who returns from Ireland and reshapes the state); Charles I (The king who dies with dignity on the scaffold)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A young man should leave his books and take up arms.
Cromwell bursts from private life like lightning.
He returns from Ireland after a harsh campaign.
King Charles dies on the scaffold (the execution platform) with courage and dignity.
The poem says old rights fall when men are too weak to hold them.
It warns Cromwell that the sword which won power must keep it.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1624 (Sort Year: 1624)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Donne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twenty three prose meditations written while Donne recovered from a grave illness.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both are wrong for a year and for the death. Donne wrote it in December 1623 and published it in 1624. He died in 1631. The full title adds and several steps in my sickness.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Donne (The sick speaker, dean of Saint Paul's, reflecting on pain and death)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In late 1623 Donne nearly died of a serious fever.
He wrote a meditation, a complaint, and a prayer for each stage of the illness.
There are 23 parts, one for each day of the sickness.
The book was entered for printing in January 1624 and published that year.
Meditation 17 says that each death touches every person.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Don Quixote

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1605 (Sort Year: 1605)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Miguel de Cervantes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor gentleman reads knight books, becomes Don Quixote, and rides out with Sancho Panza.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Part One was published in 1605. Part Two was published in 1615. Thomas Shelton's English Part One appeared in 1612. His Part Two appeared in 1620. A false Part Two by Alonso Fernandez de Avellaneda came out in 1614. The database life dates 1603 to 1625 are the period, not Cervantes's life. He lived from 1547 to 1616.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Don Quixote (Alonso Quixano, a minor noble who thinks he is a wandering knight.); Sancho Panza (The practical farm neighbour who serves as his squire.); Dulcinea del Toboso (The farm woman Aldonza Lorenzo, renamed as his ideal lady.); Cide Hamete Benengeli (The made up historian whom the narrator pretends to translate.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Full title: The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha.
It is a Spanish novel in two volumes.
He recruits a simple farmer Sancho Panza as his squire.
It had a major influence on the literary community as evidence by direct references in Alexandre Dumas' The three Musketeers (1844), Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), and Edmond Roastand's Cyrano de Bergerac (1897), as well as the word "Quixotic".
Arthur Schopenhauer cited "Don Quixote" as one of the four greatest novels ever written along with Tristam Shandy, La Nouvelle Heloise and Wilhelm Meister.
In this book Cervantes coined the popular phrase "The proof is in the pudding" and "who walks much and reads much, knows much and sees much".
Alonso Quixano reads so many knight tales that he loses hold of the real world.
He takes the name Don Quixote and calls his thin horse Rocinante.
He renames a farm woman Dulcinea del Toboso, his ideal lady.
He attacks windmills, thinking they are giants, and takes inns for castles.
Sancho Panza joins as his squire (a knight's servant) and hopes for a governorship.
Friends later trick him home.
In Part Two, readers of Part One mock the pair.
He is defeated, comes home, and dies as Alonso Quixano.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Epigrams

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1616 (Sort Year: 1616)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of short poems that praise friends and mock fools, collected in the 1616 folio.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The authorised collection is in the 1616 folio. Wikisource and one Wikipedia list also mark Epigrams 1612. For the exam, pair Epigrams with The Forest in 1616. On My First Son concerns the child who died in 1603.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ben Jonson (The poet who praises, mourns, and attacks in his own voice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jonson calls the epigram the ripest fruit of his studies.
Many pieces attack nameless courtiers, spies, and pretenders.
Poems of praise name real people, including his teacher William Camden.
On My First Son mourns his boy Benjamin, who died of plague in 1603.
The collection stands in the 1616 folio beside The Forest.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Holy Sonnets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1633 (Sort Year: 1633)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Donne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Religious sonnets in which a fearful speaker argues with God about sin and death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not a year. The first print is in Poems (1633), after Donne died, so the posthumous mark is right for this work. The 1633 book has twelve sonnets. Death, be not proud and Batter my heart are in that book. Three further sonnets stayed in manuscript longer.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A sinful soul begging God to break and remake him); Death (Addressed as a proud enemy who will himself die)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Donne wrote most of these sonnets around 1609 and 1610, before he became a priest.
One sonnet mourns his wife Anne, who died in 1617.
Friends copied the poems by hand.
He did not print them.
Twelve sonnets appeared in Poems in 1633, two years after his death.
Later copies and editions raise the usual modern set to nineteen poems.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: New Atlantis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1626 (Sort Year: 1626)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Bacon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A utopian tale of the island Bensalem, ruled by learning in Salomon's House.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the writing to about 1614. It dates the printing to 1626, after Bacon died. Wikipedia also lists 1626. Some exam books say 1627. The work is unfinished.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A European sailor who describes the visit to Bensalem); The Father of Salomon's House (A scientist priest who explains the research college)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This work is like Utopia, a fragmentary sketch of Baconian Utopia.
He tells how by accident a ship's party comes to a land in which there was a great college of science, which he begins to describe.
This dream was to be partly fulfilled in the foundation of Royal society in 1662.
It is about inhabitants of 'Bensalem' that means 'Son of Peace'. Bensalem is described as a 'Utopian City' where inhabitants are described as having a high moral character and honesty. There is a description of Solomon's House in this book.
Sailors from Peru are driven by a storm to the unknown island of Bensalem.
The people receive them kindly and keep them in the Strangers' House.
A governor explains their secret laws and their Christian revelation.
A father of Salomon's House describes laboratories, gardens, and collectors of knowledge.
The story breaks off unfinished.
It is a plan for cooperative science.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Othello

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1622 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1622)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A cunning ensign manipulates a heroic general into believing his faithful wife is unchaste.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1603. Composed c. 1603-1604 and performed in 1604. First printed in Quarto in 1622.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Othello (A Moorish general in the Venetian army consumed by jealousy); Desdemona (Othello's devoted, innocent Venetian wife); Iago (Othello's trusted, malicious ensign who manipulates everyone); Emilia (Iago's outspoken wife and Desdemona's attendant); Cassio (Othello's honourable young lieutenant)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Othello, a noble Moorish general of Venice, secretly marries the Venetian lady Desdemona.
Othello names Cassio as his lieutenant, enraging his ensign Iago.
Iago constructs a vicious plot to convince Othello that Desdemona is sleeping with Cassio.
Iago obtains Desdemona's cherished handkerchief and leaves it in Cassio's chamber.
Blind with jealousy, Othello smothers Desdemona in her bridal bed.
Emilia unmasks Iago's villainy, and Othello stabs himself in despair.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Philaster

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1620 (Sort Year: 1620)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragicomedy in which the true heir Philaster wins the princess after a false scandal.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Scholars place the play about 1609. Thomas Walkley printed the first edition in 1620. A corrected second printing came in 1622.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philaster (The true heir of Sicily, living at the king's court); Arethusa (The king's daughter, who loves Philaster); Bellario (Philaster's page, later revealed as the woman Euphrasia); Pharamond (The Spanish prince whom the king wants as his heir)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The king of Sicily plans to marry his daughter Arethusa to the Spanish prince Pharamond.
Arethusa loves Philaster, the true heir, and he sends his page Bellario to her.
Pharamond spreads a lie that Arethusa and Bellario are lovers.
Philaster believes the lie and wounds Arethusa during a hunt.
Bellario is revealed as Euphrasia, a woman in disguise, and Philaster is restored.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Songs and Sonnets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1633 (Sort Year: 1633)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Donne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A group of love lyrics that range from mockery to deep mutual love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not a year. Encyclopedia.com says the lyrics were first published in Poems (1633). The heading Songs and Sonnets was first used in the 1635 edition. The posthumous mark fits the 1633 book. It does not mean every poem was written after 1631.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A witty lover whose tone shifts from poem to poem); The Sun (Scolded as a busy intruder in The Sun Rising)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Donne wrote these lyrics mainly from the 1590s to about 1617.
Only a few appeared in print while he lived.
Friends passed handwritten copies among patrons.
The poems were first collected in Poems in 1633, after his death.
The familiar heading Songs and Sonnets was used for them in the 1635 edition.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Advancement of Learning

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1605 (Sort Year: 1605)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Bacon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A survey of all learning, dedicated to King James, which defends study and maps its branches.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both opened sources date the English book to 1605. The Latin enlargement, De Augmentis Scientiarum, appeared in 1623. Do not confuse the two dates.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Francis Bacon (The author, addressing King James I)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In this work, Bacon tries to encourage King James I to support some immortal work that contains the philosophy of Bacon, systematizing his ideas for the reform and revival of knowledge. It is divided into 2 parts.
Full Title - "Of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, Divine and Human"
It was written in the form of a letter to King James I.
He divided human understanding in three parts - i) History, related to man's faculty of memory, ii) Poetry, related to man's faculty of imagination, iii) Philosophy - Man's faculty of reason.
Bacon answers people who say that too much learning leads to atheism or unrest.
He says knowledge should glorify God and ease human suffering.
He divides learning into history, poetry, and philosophy.
He lists the gaps in each field and asks the king to support research.
In 1623 he published a longer Latin version, De Augmentis Scientiarum.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Alchemist

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1612 (Sort Year: 1612)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three cheats use a London house during the plague to sell false gold and false hopes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was acted in 1610 by the King's Men. Plague sent the first performance to Oxford, with London performances later that year. The quarto was printed in 1612. The exam year 1610 is the acting year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Face (The butler Jeremy in disguise, leader of the cheats); Subtle (The pretended alchemist); Dol Common (Their partner, who plays several false ladies); Sir Epicure Mammon (A knight who hungers for the philosopher's stone); Lovewit (The master of the house, who returns and profits)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
9. Bartholomew Fair 10. Less Powerful 11. The Devil is an Ass 12. The Staple of Knews 13. The Tale of a Tub 14. Catiline His Conspiracy - Tragedy 15. Sejanus His Fall - Tragedy 16. Eastward Ho (along with Marston and Chapman) 17. The Poetaster 18. Song to Celia 19. The Magnetic Lad 1. Every Man in His Humour (1598)
It is his first play, played by Lord Chamberlin's Men at Curtain Theatre.
The prologue of the play attacks themes and conventions of contemporary drama and explains his theory of humour.
Shakespeare acted in it (He played the role of the character Edward Knowell).
The character Bobadill is one of Jonson greatest creations, a boastful cowardly soldier.
Charles Dickens acted the role of Captain Bobadill in Ben Jonson's Every Man in his Humour, in 1845. Plot:.
In the prologue, the speaker announces that the play was written due to the popularity of the theatre.
The opening scene finds Knowell, an old man, at his house. He tells Brainworm, his servant, to fetch his son, Edward. The father is happy that Edward is a scholar, as he himself once was, but he does not approve of his son's taste for the "fruitless" arts.
Master Stephen, an easily duped countryman, then arrives to visit relatives. Knowell gives him advice on how to be a better man.
Shortly thereafter, Stephen departs. A servant then gives Knowell a letter meant for Edward. When he reads it, he realizes it is not for him and takes offense at the impolite, informal tone of the letter. He has the letter given to his son and decides he will encourage him, but not force him, to try to be a good man.
The next scene of Act I finds Edward receiving the letter and learning that his father has read it. Stephen enters and asks about the man who delivered the letter, who is now long gone. Stephen and Edward, who are cousins, talk and then go to the city to meet the man who sent the letter.
Scene three introduces the characters Mathew and Cob at the latter's house. Cob talks about respectable ancestors and Mathew asks about locating a man named Captain Bobadill, whom Cob says is his guest. Mathew does not believe this. Cob tells him the man slept on his bench the previous night. Cob ends the scene with a monologue that tells of the drama in his house and of Bobadill owing him money.
Scene four, the final scene of Act I, unfolds in Cob's house, where Bobadill lies on the bench. Mathew and Bobadill talk and Mathew agrees not to mention that Bobadill spent the night there. Mathew shares a new play, which they discuss before leaving for a tavern.
Act II opens in another part of the city. Kitely, a merchant, enters, along with his cashier, Cash, and Kitley's brother-in-law, Downright, who is a squire. Kitely tells the squire that Wellbred, his brother, has been disrespectful. Wellbred is angered.
Bobadill and Mathew look for, but do not find Wellbred. Next, in the moorfields of London, Brainworm is disguised as a soldier. He wants to stop Knowell's pursuit of his son.
Stephen and Knowell enter. Stephen has lost a purse containing a ring from his mistress.
In Act III Mathew, Bobadill, and Wellbred are in a tavern. While Mathew and Bobadill talk of disliking Wellbred's brother, Downright, Edward and Stephen arrive. Wellbred, it turns out, is the one who wrote the letter to Edward.
They go on to discuss Stephen and Bobadill's military experiences. Cash and Kitely are engaged in a shady exchange of money. Kitely sends Cash on another job and asks to be informed if Wellbred or anyone else comes to his house. An upset Cob enters and Cash tells him it is his "humour" that is making him feel distressed.
The next scene is at Justice Clement's house. Cob tells Kitely that some men have arrived at his house and Kitely worries about his wife and sister giving in to their desires. Cob attempts to put his mind at ease. Cob also wants revenge, as Bobadill has used his wife. Justice Clement and Roger his clerk arrive. Cob asks the Justice to punish Bobadill, but the Justice orders Cob jailed for his character and previous actions.
The final act, takes place at the home of Justice Clement. Clement, Knowell, Kitely, Dame Kitely, Cash, Cob, and some servants enter. They are trying to sift through the sequence of false messages they have received. Bobadill and Mathew join the group and announce they have a warrant for Downright.
Stephen, Downright, and Brainworm, who is in disguise, also arrive. Clement wants Brainworm jailed for not serving warrants in the right way.
Brainworm reveals himself and his deceitful actions are exposed. In attempting to bring closure to everything, Justice Clement instructs every person to rid themselves of the emotions that are weighing them down and they start to celebrate.
The Alchemist, a comedy in five acts by Ben Jonson, was performed in 1610 and published in 1612.
The play concerns the turmoil of deception that ensues when Lovewit leaves his London house in the care of his scheming servant, Face.
With the aid of a fraudulent alchemist named Subtle and his companion, Dol Common, Face sets about dispensing spurious charms and services to a steady stream of dupes. These include the intemperate knight Sir Epicure Mammon, the pretentious Puritans Ananias and Tribulation Wholesome, the ambitious tobacconist Abel Drugger, the gamester law clerk Dapper, and the parvenu Kastril with his widowed sister, Pliant.
The shrewd gambler Surly nearly exposes the sham by posing as a Spanish don seeking the hand of Pliant, but the gullible parties reject his accusations.
When Lovewit reappears without warning, Subtle and Dol flee the scene, leaving Face to make peace by arranging the marriage of his master to the beautiful and wealthy Dame Pliant.
Lovewit leaves town because of plague and puts his butler Jeremy in charge.
Jeremy becomes Face and joins Subtle the fake alchemist and Dol Common.
They trick a clerk, a shopkeeper, greedy Puritans, and Sir Epicure Mammon.
Mammon dreams the philosopher's stone will bring him endless wealth and pleasure.
Lovewit returns, the cheats scatter, and the master keeps the widow and the goods.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Changeling

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1653 (Sort Year: 1653)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Middleton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Beatrice Joanna hires De Flores to kill her unwanted bridegroom, then cannot escape him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Master of the Revels licensed the play on 7 May 1622. Britannica gives the print year as 1653, and the database agrees. A Wikipedia sentence says 1652, but the same page shows a 1653 title page. The main plot comes from a 1621 story book by John Reynolds.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Beatrice Joanna (Vermandero's daughter, who plots a murder so she can marry Alsemero.); De Flores (The servant who kills Alonzo and then claims Beatrice.); Alsemero (The man Beatrice loves and later marries.); Alonzo de Piracquo (The suitor her father chose, and the man De Flores murders.); Isabella (The doctor's wife in the madhouse plot.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Beatrice Joanna loves Alsemero, but her father has promised her to Alonzo.
She asks De Flores, a servant she hates, to murder Alonzo.
De Flores kills Alonzo and then demands Beatrice herself as payment.
She tries to hide the crime before the wedding night.
A second plot, in a madhouse, shows pretend fools and secret lovers.
The truth comes out, and the main plot ends in death.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Duchess of Malfi

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Webster

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A widowed duchess secretly marries her steward, and her brothers destroy her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not a year. Britannica and Wikipedia agree on publication in 1623. It was acted at Blackfriars, then at the Globe, in 1613 or 1614. The database calls the play posthumous. That is wrong. Webster was still alive.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Duchess of Malfi (A noble widow who marries for love and dies still proud); Antonio Bologna (Her steward and secret husband); Ferdinand (Her twin brother, Duke of Calabria, who goes mad); The Cardinal (Her cold, corrupt brother); Daniel de Bosola (A bitter spy and killer who later wants revenge for her); Cariola (The Duchess's waiting woman, who dies with her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The widowed Duchess loves Antonio, her honest steward.
Her brothers, Ferdinand and the Cardinal, forbid her to marry again.
They set Bosola to spy on her, and she bears three children in secret.
Ferdinand rages, and Bosola helps to imprison and strangle her.
Ferdinand goes mad, and Bosola, the brothers, and Antonio all die.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Dutch Courtezan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1605 (Sort Year: 1605)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Marston

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A London comedy about a man who leaves a paid lover for a wife.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database gives no year. The 1605 printing is certain. Leeds and Britannica place the first acting around 1604, before that printing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Freevill (A young man who leaves Franceschina to marry Beatrice); Franceschina (The Dutch courtesan who wants Freevill dead); Malheureux (Freevill's moral friend, who is tempted by Franceschina); Beatrice (The modest woman Freevill intends to marry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Freevill plans to marry Beatrice, but he still visits Franceschina.
Franceschina is a Dutch courtesan, a woman paid for sex.
His strict friend Malheureux meets her and begins to desire her.
Franceschina tries to make Malheureux kill Freevill.
Freevill pretends to be dead, the plot is exposed, and he marries Beatrice.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Forest

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1616 (Sort Year: 1616)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Fifteen poems in the 1616 folio, including the country house poem To Penshurst.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Wikisource place The Forest in 1616, in the first folio of Jonson's Works. It was printed with the Epigrams. Underwood is a later and larger collection.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ben Jonson (The poet speaking to patrons, friends, and Celia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Forest is a small book of poems inside the 1616 Works.
Most poems address patrons, the nobles who supported Jonson.
To Penshurst praises the Sidney house as generous, ordered, and unshowy.
A song to Celia, Come, my Celia, also appears in Volpone.
The book is lyric and moral, not a play.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Garden

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1681 (Sort Year: 1681)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Andrew Marvell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A speaker chooses a quiet garden over love, fame, and public life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The year of writing is debated, so it is marked unknown. The database shows only the Jacobean span. The poem was first printed in Miscellaneous Poems in 1681.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A man who prefers the garden to love and public ambition)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker leaves fame and busy society for a quiet garden.
He says trees please him more than lovers do.
Ripe fruit falls into his hands, and he stumbles on the grass.
His mind withdraws into a green thought in a green shade.
He imagines Eden before Eve, a paradise of solitude.
A flower sundial brings human time back at the end.

items.title: "The Knight of the Burning Pestle" (1613) — Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Knight of the Burning Pestle

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1613 (Sort Year: 1613)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A grocer and his wife interrupt a play and make their apprentice act as a knight.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Francis Beaumont wrote it alone. It was acted in 1607 and printed in 1613 for Walter Burre.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rafe (The grocer's apprentice, who plays a wandering knight); The Citizen (A grocer in the audience who climbs on stage and changes the play); The Citizen's Wife (Nell, who sits on stage and demands heroic scenes for Rafe); Jasper (A merchant's apprentice who loves Luce); Luce (The merchant's daughter, who chooses Jasper)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A grocer and his wife interrupt a play called The London Merchant.
They send their apprentice Rafe on stage as a knight with a burning pestle on his shield.
In the inner play, the apprentice Jasper loves his master's daughter Luce.
Rafe's fake adventures mock old romance plays and citizen plays about shop workers.
Jasper wins Luce, and the grocer's family demands a grand death scene for Rafe.

items.title: "The Maid’s Tragedy" (1619) — Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Maid’s Tragedy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1619 (Sort Year: 1619)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A king forces a marriage to hide his mistress, and the revenge ends in several deaths.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was acted about 1610 by the King's Men. The first printing is 1619.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amintor (The courtier forced to marry Evadne though he loves Aspatia); Evadne (Melantius's sister, the king's mistress, who later kills the king); Aspatia (Amintor's first love, who dies after a fight in male dress); Melantius (Evadne's brother, a general who drives the revenge); The King (The ruler of Rhodes who arranged the false marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The king of Rhodes orders Amintor to marry Evadne, though he was pledged to Aspatia.
On the wedding night Evadne refuses Amintor, because she is the king's mistress.
Her brother Melantius learns the truth and pushes her to kill the king.
Evadne ties the king to the bed and stabs him.
Aspatia dies in a disguised fight, Evadne kills herself, and Amintor dies too.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Malcontent

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1604 (Sort Year: 1604)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Marston

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A duke who has lost his throne returns in disguise and wins it by wit.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Printed in 1604, which is the exam year. Folger allows a first acting from 1602 to 1604. John Webster added an induction, a comic opening, when the King's Men took the play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Malevole (The bitter disguise of the true duke); Altofronto (The Duke of Genoa who lost his throne); Pietro (The duke who sits on Altofronto's throne); Mendoza (A scheming courtier who wants the crown); Aurelia (Pietro's unfaithful wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Altofronto, the true Duke of Genoa, disguises himself as Malevole.
Malevole is a rude man who mocks the court.
He watches Pietro, the man who holds the throne, and the lust around him.
The schemer Mendoza tries to seize power.
Malevole turns their plots against them and reveals that he is Altofronto.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Rape of Lucrece

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1594 (Quarto) (Sort Year: 1594)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A noble Roman wife kills herself after an evil prince attacks her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1593, but the first quarto was published in 1594. Richard Field printed it in London.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucrece (A virtuous Roman noblewoman); Tarquin (The tyrannical prince of Rome who attacks Lucrece); Collatine (Lucrece's loving husband); Brutus (The Roman leader who avenges Lucrece and expels the kings)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tarquin is the prince of Rome.
He visits the house of his friend Collatine.
He is overcome by lust for Collatine's virtuous wife, Lucrece.
Tarquin assaults Lucrece in the middle of the night.
Lucrece reveals the crime to her husband and father.
She then stabs herself to protect her honour.
Brutus leads the Roman people to banish the royal family and establish a republic.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Shoemaker’s Holiday

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1600 (Sort Year: 1600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Dekker

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A London shoemaker becomes Lord Mayor while lovers in disguise find a happy ending.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Admiral's Men (a London acting company) acted it in 1599. It was printed in 1600. The database files the play under fiction. It is a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Simon Eyre (The jolly shoemaker who rises to Lord Mayor); Rowland Lacy (A gentleman who disguises himself as the Dutch shoemaker Hans); Rose Otley (The Lord Mayor's daughter, loved by Lacy); Ralph (A shoemaker sent to war, who returns to his wife Jane); Jane (Ralph's wife, nearly pushed into a second marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Simon Eyre, a London shoemaker, rises to become Lord Mayor.
Rowland Lacy disguises himself as a Dutch shoemaker to stay near Rose.
Ralph the shoemaker goes to war, and his wife Jane is told he is dead.
Jane nearly marries another man, but Ralph returns and they reunite.
The king blesses the lovers, and the play celebrates work and holiday.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Tenth Muse

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1650 (Sort Year: 1650)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anne Bradstreet

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1650 book of poems by a woman poet of colonial Massachusetts.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database shows the Jacobean span, not the print year. Stephen Bowtell printed the book in London in 1650. A revised book, Several Poems, followed in 1678.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anne Bradstreet (The poet who speaks in her own voice in the prologue); Old England (A speaker in the dialogue about the troubles of 1642); New England (The colonial voice that answers Old England)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens with a prologue in the poet's own voice.
In that prologue, obnoxious means open to blame, not hateful.
She asks pardon for writing on wars, kings, and history.
Long poems debate four elements, four humours (character types), four ages, and four seasons.
A history poem covers Assyria, Persia, Greece, and Rome.
Old England and New England speak about the troubles of 1642.
She also praises Sidney, the French poet Du Bartas, and Queen Elizabeth.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The White Devil

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1612 (Sort Year: 1612)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Webster

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Vittoria and Duke Brachiano pursue a guilty love, and revenge destroys the court.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not a year. The play was acted and printed in 1612 at the Red Bull by Queen Anne's Men. The database calls it posthumous. That is wrong. Webster died about 1632.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Vittoria Corombona (A Venetian woman whose love and trial drive the plot); Brachiano (The Duke who leaves his wife Isabella for Vittoria); Flamineo (Vittoria's brother and Brachiano's scheming secretary); Monticelso (A cardinal who judges Vittoria and later becomes pope); Francisco de Medici (Duke of Florence and Isabella's brother, who plots revenge); Lodovico (A banished count who helps to kill Brachiano)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Brachiano loves Vittoria, though both are already married.
Her brother Flamineo helps the affair so he may rise at court.
Brachiano has Vittoria's husband and his own wife murdered.
Vittoria is tried and sent away, then she and the Duke flee and marry.
Francisco and Lodovico poison Brachiano and kill Vittoria and Flamineo.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Timber, or Discoveries

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1641 (Sort Year: 1641)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A posthumous notebook of remarks on writing, people, and the art of judgment.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia lists Timber, or Discoveries as London, 1641, inside the posthumous folio. That folio is often dated 1640 to 1641. Wikisource lists the title with the later works. Jonson died in 1637, so the book is posthumous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ben Jonson (The note taker, speaking from his reading and his stage experience)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jonson kept notes from his reading and from his life in the theatre.
The book was printed after his death, in the later folio.
He says a person's language shows the person most clearly.
He remembers Shakespeare as honest and free, and wishes he had blotted a thousand lines.
The notes are reflections, not a finished system of criticism.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: To His Coy Mistress

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1681 (Sort Year: 1681)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Andrew Marvell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lover begs a shy woman to love him now, because life is short.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database gives no real year, only the Jacobean span. The poem probably belongs to the Nun Appleton years. It was first printed in 1681, after Marvell died.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A lover who argues that delay will end in the grave); The Coy Mistress (The shy woman he addresses and tries to persuade)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker tells a shy lady he would court her slowly if time allowed.
He says he could praise her body for hundreds of years.
But he hears time's chariot, and he sees a vast desert ahead.
He says the grave is private, yet no lovers embrace there.
He begs her to love him now, while both of them are young.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Twelfth Night

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A shipwrecked maiden disguises herself as a male page and falls in love with her master.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1603. It was staged on Candlemas in February 1602. First printed in the 1623 Folio.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Viola (Cesario) (A shipwrecked noblewoman dressed as a male page); Duke Orsino (The love-sick Duke of Illyria); Countess Olivia (A wealthy lady in mourning who loves Cesario); Sebastian (Viola's twin brother who arrives in Illyria); Malvolio (Olivia's pompous and puritanical steward); Feste (A witty, singing fool serving Olivia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viola survives a shipwreck in Illyria and thinks her twin brother Sebastian has drowned.
She disguises herself as a young youth named Cesario to serve Duke Orsino.
Orsino sends Cesario to court Countess Olivia, but Olivia falls in love with Cesario instead.
Viola secretly suffers from her own unexpressed love for Orsino.
Mischievous household servants fool the steward Malvolio with a fake love letter.
Sebastian arrives safely in Illyria, Olivia weds him by mistake, and Orsino happily marries Viola.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Underwood

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1640 (Sort Year: 1640)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A large mixed book of later poems, printed in 1640 after Jonson's death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Wikisource date Underwood to the 1640 folio, after Jonson's death in 1637. It is not in the 1616 book. The Forest is the 1616 collection.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ben Jonson (The poet of the later lyrics, odes, and elegies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Underwood gathers poems that did not fit in the 1616 Forest.
It includes love poems in A Celebration of Charis.
It includes religious poems and poems of praise.
The ode for Cary and Morison says a short noble life can outrank a long one.
The book appeared in the posthumous folio.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: King Lear

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1608 (Quarto 1), 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1608)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An aging monarch divides his kingdom among flattering daughters and descends into tragic madness.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1603, which is too early. Lear was written c. 1605-1606 and first printed in 1608.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Lear (The tragic aging King of Britain driven mad by grief); Cordelia (Lear's truthful, loyal youngest daughter); Goneril (Lear's cruel eldest daughter); Regan (Lear's ruthless second daughter); The Fool (Lear's insightful jester who speaks uncomfortable truths); Edmund (Gloucester's treacherous bastard son who plots against his family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King Lear asks his three daughters to proclaim their love before dividing his realm.
Goneril and Regan offer lavish flattery, but Cordelia speaks honestly and is banished.
Lear gives his lands to Goneril and Regan, who promptly strip him of power and dignity.
Cast out during a raging storm on the heath, Lear falls into deep madness.
Cordelia returns with a French army to save her father, but their forces are defeated.
Cordelia is executed in prison, and heartbroken Lear dies while weeping over her body.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Antony and Cleopatra

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Roman ruler sacrifices his empire and life for his passionate bond with Egypt's queen.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1606-1607 and First Folio 1623, which is correct. Registered in May 1608.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mark Antony (A Roman triumvir torn between imperial duty and passion); Cleopatra (The proud, majestic Queen of Egypt); Octavius Caesar (The ambitious Roman ruler who becomes Emperor Augustus); Enobarbus (Antony's cynical lieutenant who famously describes Cleopatra)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mark Antony lives in luxury in Alexandria with his lover Queen Cleopatra.
Antony journeys to Rome and marries Octavia to preserve peace with Octavius Caesar.
Antony soon abandons Octavia to return to Cleopatra in Egypt, provoking open war.
At the naval Battle of Actium, Cleopatra flees and Antony pursues her, suffering defeat.
Antony falls upon his sword after receiving a false report of Cleopatra's death.
Cleopatra applies poisonous asps to her breast to avoid being paraded through Rome.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Macbeth

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A brave Scottish general murders his king to take the throne and becomes a bloodthirsty tyrant.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1603, which is too early. Written c. 1606 after the 1605 Gunpowder Plot to honor King James I. First printed in the First Folio.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Macbeth (A Scottish general whose vaulting ambition destroys him); Lady Macbeth (Macbeth's determined wife who urges him to regicide); The Three Witches (Supernatural sisters who provide ambiguous prophecies); Banquo (Macbeth's noble comrade whose heirs are prophesied to be kings); Macduff (The Thane of Fife who slays the tyrant Macbeth)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Three weird sisters prophesy that Macbeth will become Thane of Cawdor and King of Scotland.
Lady Macbeth goads her husband into stabbing King Duncan in his sleep at their castle.
Macbeth seizes the crown, but tortured by paranoia, orders the murder of his friend Banquo.
Banquo's ghost terrorises Macbeth at a royal feast, breaking Macbeth's composure.
Lady Macbeth goes mad with guilt, tries to wash phantom blood from her hands, and dies.
Macduff slays Macbeth in battle, and Duncan's son Malcolm is crowned rightful king.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Volpone

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1607 (Sort Year: 1607)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rich Venetian pretends to be dying so that greedy heirs will bring him gifts.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play page dates the Globe premiere to spring 1606. The author page says it was acted in 1605 and printed in 1607. The quarto is early 1607. Use 1606 for the stage and 1607 for the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Volpone (The fox, a childless magnifico who fakes his deathbed); Mosca (The fly, his parasite servant, who outgrows him); Celia (Corvino's honest wife, offered to Volpone); Corvino (The crow, a jealous merchant who will sell his wife's honour); Bonario (Corbaccio's son, who saves Celia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Volpone, the fox, worships his gold and feigns a fatal illness.
Mosca, the fly, tells Voltore, Corbaccio, and Corvino that each will inherit.
Corvino is tricked into offering his wife Celia.
Volpone tries to force Celia, and her rescuer Bonario is then framed in court.
Volpone names Mosca his heir as a joke, loses control, and both are punished.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sonnets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1609 (Quarto) (Sort Year: 1609)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A collection of 154 sonnets exploring beauty, destructive time, a young nobleman, and a dark lady.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives 1609. Thomas Thorpe published the quarto in 1609, but the poems circulated in private manuscript in the 1590s.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Poet (The speaker meditating on beauty, art, time, and love); The Fair Youth (An attractive young nobleman addressed in sonnets 1 to 126); The Dark Lady (A dark-complexioned woman addressed in sonnets 127 to 152); The Rival Poet (A competing poet who also seeks the patron's favor)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sonnets 1 to 17 urge a beautiful young man to marry and preserve his youth in offspring.
Sonnets 18 to 126 address the Fair Youth, celebrating love and defying time through poetry.
Sonnets 127 to 152 turn to the Dark Lady, depicting stormy sensual passion and moral distress.
Sonnets 153 and 154 offer lighthearted mythological adaptations of Cupid's fire.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Winter’s Tale

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A king's destructive jealousy tears his family apart until sixteen years of repentance bring a miraculous reunion.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1609-1611 and First Folio 1623, which is correct. No early quarto exists.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leontes (The King of Sicily whose sudden jealousy ruins his kingdom); Hermione (The virtuous Queen of Sicily whose statue comes to life); Perdita (The abandoned Sicilian princess raised in Bohemia); Florizel (The Bohemian prince who loves Perdita); Paulina (Hermione's courageous and loyal defender); Autolycus (A roguish, musical peddler and pickpocket)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King Leontes of Sicily wrongly suspects his queen Hermione of adultery with his friend King Polixenes.
Leontes throws pregnant Hermione into prison and commands her newborn daughter Perdita abandoned.
Apollo's oracle declares Hermione chaste, but Leontes' young son dies, and Hermione seemingly dies of sorrow.
Perdita is found and raised by an old shepherd in Bohemia.
Sixteen years later, Polixenes' son Florizel falls in love with the shepherdess Perdita.
The lovers journey to Sicily, where Leontes welcomes them, and Hermione's statue miraculously comes alive.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Tempest

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1623 (First Folio) (Sort Year: 1623)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An exiled sorcerer shipwrecks his enemies on a magic island and chooses forgiveness over vengeance.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database sort_year is 1603, which is too early. Written c. 1610-1611 using Strachey's 1610 letter about the 1609 Bermuda wreck. First printed in the 1623 Folio.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prospero (The banished Duke of Milan and master of magic); Miranda (Prospero's gentle daughter who has lived on the island since childhood); Ariel (A spirit of the air bound to serve Prospero); Caliban (The savage native inhabitant of the island); Ferdinand (The prince of Naples who wins Miranda's love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Prospero, the rightful Duke of Milan, lives stranded on an island with his daughter Miranda.
He summons a magical storm to shipwreck his treacherous brother Antonio and King Alonso.
Alonso's gentle son Ferdinand survives and falls deeply in love with Miranda.
The airy spirit Ariel serves Prospero, while the native monster Caliban plots rebellion.
Prospero brings his foes before him, pardons their past crimes, and renounces his magic art.
Prospero prepares to sail home to Italy, having freed Ariel from bondage.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poly-Olbion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1612 (Sort Year: 1612)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Michael Drayton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem that tours the counties, rivers, and legends of England and Wales.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1612 is only part one, songs 1 to 18. That part was issued again in 1613. Part two, twelve more songs, was printed in 1622. John Selden supplied prose notes to the first part.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Poet (The speaker who travels in imagination through Britain); The Genius of the Place (The ancient spirit of the island, asked to guide the poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet calls on the genius of the island, its ancient local spirit.
Each song describes one county or more, and the rivers speak as nymphs.
A nymph here is a female spirit of nature.
Songs 1 to 18 were printed in 1612, with maps by William Hole.
Twelve further songs were printed in 1622. The planned songs on Scotland were never written.

items.title: "The Two Noble Kinsmen (with Fletcher)" (1634 (Quarto)) — William Shakespeare

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Two Noble Kinsmen (with Fletcher)

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1634 (Quarto) (Sort Year: 1634)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Shakespeare

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two devoted cousins and knights become bitter rivals when they both fall in love with the same princess.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database gives c. 1613-1614 and print 1634, which is correct. The play was not included in the 1623 First Folio.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Palamon (A Theban knight who loves Emilia); Arcite (Palamon's cousin and romantic rival); Emilia (The sister-in-law of Theseus loved by both knights); Theseus (Duke of Athens who commands the tournament); The Jailer's Daughter (A young woman who goes mad for unrequited love of Palamon)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Palamon and Arcite are noble cousins from Thebes imprisoned in Athens.
From their cell window they glimpse Princess Emilia and both instantly fall in love with her.
Their deep bond of friendship breaks as each claims her as his own.
Arcite is banished, while a jailer's daughter frees Palamon out of desperate love.
Duke Theseus arranges a formal tournament where the victor will marry Emilia and the loser will die.
Arcite wins the combat but is fatally thrown by his horse, bestowing Emilia upon Palamon before dying.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Bartholomew Fair

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1631 (Sort Year: 1631)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ben Jonson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A noisy Smithfield fair exposes Puritans, fools, and a justice who spies in disguise.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It opened at the Hope Theatre on 31 October 1614. It was played at court the next day. Jonson started a printing in 1631 and then stopped. The play was included in the 1640 to 1641 folio.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Justice Overdo (A magistrate who spies on the fair and is humiliated); Zeal of the Land Busy (A hypocritical Puritan who rails against the puppet show); Cokes (A foolish country heir who is robbed again and again); Winwife and Quarlous (Two gallants who compete for Grace Wellborn)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is one of his most adventurous and original plays.
A fair is held annually on St. Bartholomew's day on 24th Aug.
Major Characters:.
Adam Overdo: a justice.
Bartholomew Cokes: the country squire.
Grace Wellborn: Cokes' suitor.
Wasp: Cokes' servant who has biting tongue.
Puritan Busy: he is the hypocritical person whose mind is more fixed on food than faith Sejanus His Fall (1603)
A Roman tragedy performed by the King's man at the Globe with Shakespeare and Richard Burbage in the cast.
An induction (a comic preface) makes a contract with the audience.
Littlewit, Cokes, and Justice Overdo all go to Bartholomew Fair.
Zeal of the Land Busy, a Puritan, comes to eat pork and then attacks the fair.
Overdo disguises himself, is beaten, and is put in the stocks.
A puppet show silences Busy.
Overdo reveals himself and invites everyone to supper.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Novum Organum

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1620 (Sort Year: 1620)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Francis Bacon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Latin book that teaches a new method for discovering the laws of nature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It appeared in 1620 inside Instauratio Magna (the Great Instauration). Britannica and Wikipedia agree on 1620.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bacon rejects the old habit of jumping from a few facts to a grand theory.
He names four idols, or false habits, that twist human judgment.
The idols are of the Tribe, the Cave, the Market, and the Theatre.
He asks the inquirer to collect tables of presence, absence, and degree.
True axioms (general rules) should rise slowly from those tables.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hesperides

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1648 (Sort Year: 1648)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Herrick

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A large book of short poems on love, flowers, country feasts, and the speed of time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The only book Herrick published is Hesperides, printed in London in 1648. Many poems were written earlier in Devon.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Poet (The speaker who celebrates love, flowers, and country feasts); Corinna (The woman invited to go out on May morning); The Virgins (The young women told to gather rosebuds while they may)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hesperides is Herrick's large book of short poems, printed in 1648.
Most poems praise love, flowers, country feasts, and the passing of youth.
To the Virgins tells young women to marry while they are young.
The poem on Corinna calls her out to the May feast.
Many lines were written while Herrick was vicar in Devon.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Leviathan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1651 (Sort Year: 1651)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hobbes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book on why people give power to a ruler so they can live in safety.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Hobbes finished the book by 1650. The English book appeared in 1651. A revised Latin edition came in 1668. An earlier related book, De Cive, was published in 1642.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Hobbes (The writer who argues for peace under one strong power.); The Sovereign (The person or assembly that keeps the peace and makes the law.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hobbes compares the state to a huge artificial man.
Without a common power, people live in fear of violent death.
He calls that life solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
Each person agrees to give up self rule if the others do the same.
The sovereign then holds the sword and church power together.
Subjects may resist only when the ruler cannot protect their lives.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: L’Allegro

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1645 (Sort Year: 1645)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Milton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A companion poem celebrating joy, daytime pleasures, country life, and cheerful mirth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: John Milton. The exact writing date is unknown, likely 1631-1632.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Cheerful Speaker (A lively narrator who chooses joyful company); Mirth (Euphrosyne) (The goddess of joy and celebration)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker banishes dark and loathed Melancholy.
He welcomes Mirth (Euphrosyne) and her companions, including Jest and Youth.
He walks in the countryside at dawn to watch sunrise and farm life.
He describes country dances, folklore stories, and festive town scenes.
He ends by enjoying sweet music and comic theater.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Noble Numbers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1648 (Sort Year: 1648)

fields.value: A brief epic poem in four books about Jesus resisting the temptations of Satan in the desert.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database incorrectly lists 1667 and Paradise Lost (1667. The correct publication year is 1671. It was published in one volume with Samson Agonistes.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jesus (The Son of God, who resists all of Satan's temptations); Satan (The devil, who tries to tempt Jesus in the wilderness); God the Father (The divine ruler who announces the victory of His Son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Paradise Regained is a poem by John Milton, but first published in 1671 by John Macock.
The volume which contained it, also contained Samson Agonistes; a tragic closet drama (Agonistes means wrestler/athlete/warrior).
It is a sequel of Paradise Lost written in blank verse.
It is published in 4 books.
Jesus is baptized by John the Baptist and goes into the wilderness.
Satan approaches Jesus and tempts him with food to break his fast.
Satan tempts Jesus with wealth, worldly power, and classical learning.
Jesus calmly rejects all temptations and places his trust in God.
Satan falls defeated, and angels feed Jesus and celebrate his victory.

Vaughan says a long sickness showed him a wasted youth.
He turns from idle verse and follows George Herbert.
Poems such as The World, The Retreat, and Peace seek God.
Part I came out in 1650, and a larger Part II came out in 1655.

Ferrar printed it in 1633 as The Temple.
The poems begin at The Church Porch and move through worship.
They end in peace, as in the poem Love, where Love welcomes the soul.

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Milton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A great epic poem telling the biblical story of the fall of Satan and the fall of humanity.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The 12-book second edition was published in 1674.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Satan (The proud fallen angel who leads the rebellion against God); Adam (The first man, created by God to live in Eden); Eve (The first woman, created from Adam, tempted by Satan); God the Father (The all-powerful creator of Heaven, Earth, and humanity); The Son of God (God's divine Son, who offers to sacrifice himself for humanity)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an epic poem written in blank verse in 1667.
In consisted of ten books. A second edition followed in 1674 which was arranged into twelve books. On the reader's request and also to neatly match with Virgil's Aenied which was also written into 12 books, Book VII, and Book X was split into two, thus total 12 books.
Milton's purpose to write this book as per Book I, is to "Justify the way of god to man."
In 1674 edition Milton also added an introductory prose "argument" summarizing the plot of each book to prepare readers for the complex poetry that was to follow.
In Paradise Lost, Satan takes various shapes as:.
Comet or meteor.
Cherub.
Cormorant.
Toad.
Serpent/snake Prologue.
Milton opens his poem's subject: Human kind's first act of disobedience towards god.
The act is Adam and Eve's eating forbidden fruit of the tree of knowledge.
The first book of the bible is called Genesis.
Milton asserts that the sin of Adam and Eve's brought death to human beings for the first time, causing to lose our home in paradise until Jesus comes to restore humankind to its former position of purity.
Milton's speaker announces that he wants to be inspired with this sacred knowledge because he wants to show his fellowman that the fall of humankind into sin and death was part of the god's greater plan and that god's plan is justified.
Thus prologue finishes.
Satan and his rebel angels are thrown out of Heaven into Hell.
Satan resolves to fight God by corrupting God's new creation, humankind.
God allows Satan to reach Earth, but God plans the future salvation of humanity.
Satan tempts Eve in the Garden of Eden to eat the forbidden fruit, and Adam eats it too.
Adam and Eve are driven out of Eden, but they leave with hope for the future.
